You should not be doing this anymore for macros imported from other crates, however.

Path-based scoping for declarative macros allows us to work with macros in a way which feels more idiomatic.The macro works a lot like any other item, and can be invoked before the definition.In order to be used, it needs to be manually imported or resolved from the module tree.This can be accomplished with a small bit of code right after the macro definition:macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } // Re-export as an item in the module tree. pub(crate) use helper_macro; When you do this, since the macro is now a part of the module tree, order no longer matters.// Can call here, even if the macro isn't defined yet. helper_macro!(); macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro; // Can obviously still call here. helper_macro!(); Even though you can refer to macros out of order when they use path-based scoping, you’ll probably still want to define them before they’re used within the same file. Not because it’s necessary, but because it’s readable!The real benefit of this is that other modules can import and use the macro like they would any other item.mod submodule { macro_rules! helper_macro { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro; } mod another_submodule { // You can use it like a normal item! use crate::submodule::helper_macro; helper_macro!(); // Or you can refer to it by a path! crate::submodule::helper_macro!(); } It’s most common to see this used with pub(crate), but you can really use all item visibilities here (pub(super), pub(in some::path), empty for private). pub has some strange properties, however - we’ll cover that in the next section.

It’s most common to see this used with pub(crate), but you can really use all item visibilities here (pub(super), pub(in some::path), empty for private). pub has some strange properties, however - we’ll cover that in the next section.

If you want a declarative macro to be usable from outside your crate, you have to attach the #[macro_export] attribute to it.Be careful when deciding to export a macro!After you export a macro, users may grow to depend on it, and it may become difficult to change or maintain. This is why I usually err towards not exporting a macro, until I’m sure it’s warranted.Still, if you’re sure it’s the right thing to do, you can accomplish it like so:#[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } mod submodule { use crate::exported_macro; exported_macro!(); } The observable effects of this attribute are:The root of your crate will publicly export the macro for dependents to use (use your_crate::exported_macro).You can privately import the macro using normal path-based scoping (use crate::exported_macro).It doesn’t matter whether the macro is in a submodule or not, it will always export at the root.exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` mod module { use crate::exported_macro; exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of the `use` statement mod submodule { #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of the `use` statement } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` The #[macro_use] attribute still has an effect privately within your crate, as one would expect for textual scoping rules. Though, I don’t recommend using it on modules containing exported macros, instead just go through the exported path.exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` mod module { // <- Would not be usable here without a `use` statement #[macro_use] mod submodule { #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_use]` } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` If you want to export a macro somewhere other than the crate root, there’s a way to allow for that.It would be nice if you could just not use #[macro_export], and instead pub use exported_macro, but as for now this doesn’t work. If you try it, you will be met with a compile error that the macro is “only public within the crate, and cannot be re-exported”.So, you MUST use #[macro_export] on exported macros. Then, you can bind that exported macro to a specific location in the module tree with pub use exported_macro.That’s annoying since it’ll publish a macro in the root (which you probably don’t intend), so the general pattern for this is:Hide the publicly exported macro (so folks can’t see it’s actually at the root).Create a public path binding in the module where you want the macro to be accessed from.So, for instance:pub mod submodule { // Since this is `#[macro_export]`, // it will still wind up at the crate root. // // Because of that, we name this in a way that deters usage. // We'll also hide it, so that it doesn't appear in docs. #[doc(hidden)] #[macro_export] macro_rules! __exported_macro { () => {}; } /// The actual documentation will go here! #[doc(inline)] pub use __exported_macro as exported_macro; } // Technically this does export the following macro... crate::__exported_macro!(); // However, documentation will only list this version. // And, this version will be public for dependents to use. crate::submodule::exported_macro!(); In future versions of Rust, this cruft around visibility and module tree exporting may get cleaned up.It’s hard to make changes like this to the Rust language that won’t break existing code. So this has remained one of those weird parts of the language which - if you’re not careful - can work in odd, non-idiomatic ways.There’s a pretty in-depth thread about this here on the Rust internals forum.

Though, I don’t recommend using it on modules containing exported macros, instead just go through the exported path.exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` mod module { // <- Would not be usable here without a `use` statement #[macro_use] mod submodule { #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_use]` } exported_macro!(); // <- Works because of `#[macro_export]` If you want to export a macro somewhere other than the crate root, there’s a way to allow for that.It would be nice if you could just not use #[macro_export], and instead pub use exported_macro, but as for now this doesn’t work. If you try it, you will be met with a compile error that the macro is “only public within the crate, and cannot be re-exported”.So, you MUST use #[macro_export] on exported macros. Then, you can bind that exported macro to a specific location in the module tree with pub use exported_macro.That’s annoying since it’ll publish a macro in the root (which you probably don’t intend), so the general pattern for this is:Hide the publicly exported macro (so folks can’t see it’s actually at the root).Create a public path binding in the module where you want the macro to be accessed from.So, for instance:pub mod submodule { // Since this is `#[macro_export]`, // it will still wind up at the crate root. // // Because of that, we name this in a way that deters usage. // We'll also hide it, so that it doesn't appear in docs. #[doc(hidden)] #[macro_export] macro_rules! __exported_macro { () => {}; } /// The actual documentation will go here! #[doc(inline)] pub use __exported_macro as exported_macro; } // Technically this does export the following macro... crate::__exported_macro!(); // However, documentation will only list this version. // And, this version will be public for dependents to use. crate::submodule::exported_macro!(); In future versions of Rust, this cruft around visibility and module tree exporting may get cleaned up.It’s hard to make changes like this to the Rust language that won’t break existing code. So this has remained one of those weird parts of the language which - if you’re not careful - can work in odd, non-idiomatic ways.There’s a pretty in-depth thread about this here on the Rust internals forum.

Recall from our prior article, when we talked about macro hygiene, that Rust uses what’s known as “mixed-site hygiene”.Most items - other than local variables - are resolved from where the macro is invoked (functions, types, traits, etc.). For crate-local macros, you can be a little looser with this and require that the invoking code imports some items as needed to compile. But for crate-exported macros, it’s not a good idea to force the user to do this.Because of that, you should keep the following things in mind:You usually want to avoid using the crate keyword directly, because it may not refer to your crate.Since you’re in less control over the surrounding code for crate-exported macros, you should not assume anything about what has been imported at the invocation site.For declarative macros, there’s a special, always-present meta-variable called $crate, which resolves to the crate that your declarative macro is defined in. So it’s usually prudent to use that as a common reference point for any items needed by your macro’s expansion.// Example type - pretend we have a full type definition. pub struct MyCustomHashMap { /*...*/ } /// A declarative macro that produces a hash map. /// /// Note: Actually, the standard is attempting to add this! /// See: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.hash_map.html #[macro_export] macro_rules! hash_map { ( $( $key:expr => $value:expr ),* $(,)? ) => {{ // Use our hashmap implementation from our crate. let mut map = $crate::MyCustomHashMap::new(); $( map.insert($key, $value); )* map }} } #[test] fn example() { let map = hash_map! { "key" => "value", }; assert_eq!(map.get("key"), Some(&"value")); } In the above example we demonstrate this with a MyCustomHashMap which our crate also exports. Other standing functions, or other required traits, would also need to be resolved via $crate.If your macro depends on items from other crates, it’s often wise to re-export those dependencies in a public module hidden within your crate. We usually name this something like __private and mark it #[doc(hidden)] to deter usage.#[doc(hidden)] pub mod __private { // Publicly re-export things that your macro uses here. } The serde crate does this with its own __private module. Though, their instance of it may be more for their procedural macros (Serialize and Deserialize). After all, this isn’t a problem specific to declarative macros.

Macros very often don’t have a specific type they’re bound to, usually they’re general convenience macros.That being the case, I recommend the following organization strategy:For macros which are constrained to a single module or function, just define them where they’re needed.For macros which are shared across multiple modules, define them in a common parent module.Tip: For smaller crates, this can often be easiest to target the top-most module (lib.rs).I don’t like to carelessly slap macros into some parent module (or I have several of them, which becomes unwieldy). So I put them in separate files for each macro that I define, and then re-export them into some organizational parent module.Crate-exported macros fit into this pretty well. In those cases, I just don’t re-export into the parent if the intended way to access the macro is by from the crate root.This harkens back to my module organization article, where I detail methods of using “organizational modules”, and defining types in their own separate files.Please take a look at that if you are having trouble understanding my organization strategy.mod.rs: (organizational module; often lib.rs)mod macros; mod type_a; mod type_b; mod type_c; // etc... macros/mod.rs: (organizational module)// Modules: mod exported_macro; mod helper_macro_a; mod helper_macro_b; mod helper_macro_c; // etc... // Re-Exports: pub(crate) use helper_macro_a::*; pub(crate) use helper_macro_b::*; pub(crate) use helper_macro_c::*; // etc... macros/exported_macro.rs:// In this case, I'm happy to bind it to the root. #[macro_export] macro_rules! exported_macro { () => {}; } macros/helper_macro_a.rs:macro_rules! helper_macro_a { () => {}; } pub(crate) use helper_macro_a; Elsewhere in the crate:// Either pull them in for usage: use crate::macros::{helper_macro_a, helper_macro_b}; helper_macro_a!(); helper_macro_b!(); // Or refer to them via absolute paths: crate::macros::helper_macro_c!(); I know this seems like overkill, but the nice thing about this is I can always very easily find a macro. Either the macro is defined near its usage (so it’s within the same file), or the file is named the same thing as the macro so it’s easy to open via a command.If a macro is very closely related to another macro, and they’re only split up for ease of maintenance, I usually put them in the same file. But I only do that if they are meant to be implementation details of the main macro intended to be invoked.And, you don’t always need an organizing macros module - you could just re-export the macros right into the main organizational module. That’s for each person and project to decide on.

That being the case, I recommend the following organization strategy:For macros which are constrained to a single module or function, just define them where they’re needed.For macros which are shared across multiple modules, define them in a common parent module.Tip: For smaller crates, this can often be easiest to target the top-most module (lib.rs).I don’t like to carelessly slap macros into some parent module (or I have several of them, which becomes unwieldy). Now that we know how to integrate declarative macros into our project, let’s look at some use cases for them.At the risk of sounding like a broken record - I would like to remind you to try as hard as possible NOT to export the macro.A crate-local macro, as stated, is really nice because users only depend on the side effects of it. You control the syntax and the places it’s invoked completely. There’s less to worry about with respects to breaking changes, or dependencies on unintended usage of the macro.Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

You control the syntax and the places it’s invoked completely. There’s less to worry about with respects to breaking changes, or dependencies on unintended usage of the macro.Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

There’s less to worry about with respects to breaking changes, or dependencies on unintended usage of the macro.Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

Only export a macro if you’re sure it’s a wise decision.

While developing a crate, you may author types that have some nearly-identically-implemented functions or traits.If the types are semantically closely related, we can reduce duplication using a helper macro. The helper macro will implement the common traits or function, with some information provided to it.Some specific examples of when this is beneficial include:If you need to author several types which are mostly simple wrappers of other types (something like a newtype).If you want to ensure several types have an identical subset of an API (functions and traits).Be careful not to reach for declarative macros at the smallest sign of duplication, though. Instead, you should consider it when things appear to be very cut-and-paste. If you over-generalize, that could make maintenance more of a burden, not less.For implementation macros like these, I like to follow a key = value pattern.macro_rules! impl_example { ( input_1 = $input_1:literal, input_2 = ($($input_2:tt)*), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = $grouped_input_1:literal, grouped_input_2 = $grouped_input_2:ident, grouped_input_3 = $grouped_input_3:expr, }, input_4 = [$($input_4:expr),* $(,)?], ) => { /*Expansion Here*/ }; } impl_example! { input_1 = 123, input_2 = (complex; grouped, input), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = "sample", grouped_input_2 = Sample, grouped_input_3 = concat!("..."), // ... }, input_4 = [ array_value_1, array_value_2, array_value_3, // ... ], // ... etc ... } My reason for preferring this syntax is:You cannot accidentally map a fragment to the wrong input without it being visible at the call site.It uses a different binding syntax from struct initialization to distance itself from appearing to initialize an object.Despite the binding syntax being different, it feels familiar enough to be immediately understood.Though, I’ll admit the last two points aren’t that important. If you feel more comfortable you could use a more “struct field initialization” style format (key: value). That’s up to you!Don’t over-generalize these, accept them in one order - we’re only using these internally after all.I sometimes like to order them alphanumerically by key name, so that the order is at least consistent.ExamplesAn example of this in the wild are the integer types in the Rust language itself. Integer types (like u8) use a crate-local int_impl macro to implement common functions and traits.It’s also common to use declarative macros to assist in implementing a trait across tuples of different arities. Commonly useful in cases where your trait will just call the same trait on all tuple elements. You can see an example of this in the serde crate with the crate-local tuple_impls! macro.If you’d like a toy example - here’s one using some strongly typed time values. The macro helps us ensure the conversion implementations are consistent between the different types.#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub struct OverflowError; #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Hours(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Minutes(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Seconds(u32); macro_rules! impl_time_functionality { ( from = [$($from:ty),* $(,)?], seconds_per = $seconds_per:expr, try_from = [$($try_from:ty),* $(,)?], type = $type:ty, ) => { // Ensure that we have common functions that we expect all of these time types to have. // // Reminder that you can open multiple impl blocks for a single type, so if there are // functions that don't make sense to be commonly implemented here, then just write them // in a separate impl block for the intended type outside of this macro. impl $type { // Helper constant to facilitate conversion impls. // We don't want to export it publicly from this case. pub(crate) const SECONDS_PER: u32 = $seconds_per; pub fn to_u32(self) -> u32 { self.0 } } $( impl TryFrom<$try_from> for $type { type Error = OverflowError; fn try_from(value: $try_from) -> Result { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$try_from>::SECONDS_PER > $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($try_from), " must contain more seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Ok(Self(value.to_u32() .checked_mul(<$try_from>::SECONDS_PER / Self::SECONDS_PER) .ok_or(OverflowError)?)) } } )* $( impl From<$from> for $type { fn from(value: $from) -> Self { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$from>::SECONDS_PER < $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($from), " must contain fewer seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Self(value.to_u32() / (Self::SECONDS_PER / <$from>::SECONDS_PER)) } } )* }; } impl_time_functionality! { from = [], seconds_per = 1, try_from = [ Minutes, Hours ], type = Seconds, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds ], seconds_per = 60, try_from = [ Hours ], type = Minutes, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds, Minutes ], seconds_per = 60 * 60, try_from = [], type = Hours, } #[test] fn test() { assert_eq!(Hours::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Seconds(60 * 60)); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Minutes(60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Minutes(60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Minutes(60)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Hours(1)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Minutes(60))); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); } Sometimes the deduplication is not worth the obfuscation that it creates, but that’s a case-by-case thing. For simple types like this (and the integer types from the standard library), the benefit is clear, as it produces the obvious intended end result and ensures the APIs are all implemented uniformly.If you find yourself adding a lot of special-casing and splitting your macro into many separate macros, that might be a sign that you’ve attempted to use this pattern in a place where it’s not helpful.In those cases, it’s probably best to just write out all your traits and impls by-hand, even if it results in some duplication.

Instead, you should consider it when things appear to be very cut-and-paste. If you over-generalize, that could make maintenance more of a burden, not less.For implementation macros like these, I like to follow a key = value pattern.macro_rules! impl_example { ( input_1 = $input_1:literal, input_2 = ($($input_2:tt)*), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = $grouped_input_1:literal, grouped_input_2 = $grouped_input_2:ident, grouped_input_3 = $grouped_input_3:expr, }, input_4 = [$($input_4:expr),* $(,)?], ) => { /*Expansion Here*/ }; } impl_example! { input_1 = 123, input_2 = (complex; grouped, input), input_3 = { grouped_input_1 = "sample", grouped_input_2 = Sample, grouped_input_3 = concat!("..."), // ... }, input_4 = [ array_value_1, array_value_2, array_value_3, // ... ], // ... etc ... } My reason for preferring this syntax is:You cannot accidentally map a fragment to the wrong input without it being visible at the call site.It uses a different binding syntax from struct initialization to distance itself from appearing to initialize an object.Despite the binding syntax being different, it feels familiar enough to be immediately understood.Though, I’ll admit the last two points aren’t that important. If you feel more comfortable you could use a more “struct field initialization” style format (key: value). That’s up to you!Don’t over-generalize these, accept them in one order - we’re only using these internally after all.I sometimes like to order them alphanumerically by key name, so that the order is at least consistent.ExamplesAn example of this in the wild are the integer types in the Rust language itself. Integer types (like u8) use a crate-local int_impl macro to implement common functions and traits.It’s also common to use declarative macros to assist in implementing a trait across tuples of different arities. Commonly useful in cases where your trait will just call the same trait on all tuple elements. You can see an example of this in the serde crate with the crate-local tuple_impls! macro.If you’d like a toy example - here’s one using some strongly typed time values. The macro helps us ensure the conversion implementations are consistent between the different types.#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)] pub struct OverflowError; #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Hours(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Minutes(u32); #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, Hash, Ord, PartialEq, PartialOrd)] pub struct Seconds(u32); macro_rules! impl_time_functionality { ( from = [$($from:ty),* $(,)?], seconds_per = $seconds_per:expr, try_from = [$($try_from:ty),* $(,)?], type = $type:ty, ) => { // Ensure that we have common functions that we expect all of these time types to have. // // Reminder that you can open multiple impl blocks for a single type, so if there are // functions that don't make sense to be commonly implemented here, then just write them // in a separate impl block for the intended type outside of this macro. impl $type { // Helper constant to facilitate conversion impls. // We don't want to export it publicly from this case. pub(crate) const SECONDS_PER: u32 = $seconds_per; pub fn to_u32(self) -> u32 { self.0 } } $( impl TryFrom<$try_from> for $type { type Error = OverflowError; fn try_from(value: $try_from) -> Result { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$try_from>::SECONDS_PER > $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($try_from), " must contain more seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Ok(Self(value.to_u32() .checked_mul(<$try_from>::SECONDS_PER / Self::SECONDS_PER) .ok_or(OverflowError)?)) } } )* $( impl From<$from> for $type { fn from(value: $from) -> Self { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$from>::SECONDS_PER < $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($from), " must contain fewer seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Self(value.to_u32() / (Self::SECONDS_PER / <$from>::SECONDS_PER)) } } )* }; } impl_time_functionality! { from = [], seconds_per = 1, try_from = [ Minutes, Hours ], type = Seconds, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds ], seconds_per = 60, try_from = [ Hours ], type = Minutes, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds, Minutes ], seconds_per = 60 * 60, try_from = [], type = Hours, } #[test] fn test() { assert_eq!(Hours::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Seconds(60 * 60)); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Minutes(60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Minutes(60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Minutes(60)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Hours(1)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Minutes(60))); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); } Sometimes the deduplication is not worth the obfuscation that it creates, but that’s a case-by-case thing. impl_time_functionality { ( from = [$($from:ty),* $(,)?], seconds_per = $seconds_per:expr, try_from = [$($try_from:ty),* $(,)?], type = $type:ty, ) => { // Ensure that we have common functions that we expect all of these time types to have. // // Reminder that you can open multiple impl blocks for a single type, so if there are // functions that don't make sense to be commonly implemented here, then just write them // in a separate impl block for the intended type outside of this macro. impl $type { // Helper constant to facilitate conversion impls. // We don't want to export it publicly from this case. pub(crate) const SECONDS_PER: u32 = $seconds_per; pub fn to_u32(self) -> u32 { self.0 } } $( impl TryFrom<$try_from> for $type { type Error = OverflowError; fn try_from(value: $try_from) -> Result { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$try_from>::SECONDS_PER > $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($try_from), " must contain more seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Ok(Self(value.to_u32() .checked_mul(<$try_from>::SECONDS_PER / Self::SECONDS_PER) .ok_or(OverflowError)?)) } } )* $( impl From<$from> for $type { fn from(value: $from) -> Self { // This const assert ensures we haven't used the helper macro improperly. const _: () = assert!( <$from>::SECONDS_PER < $seconds_per, concat!(stringify!($from), " must contain fewer seconds than ", stringify!($type)), ); Self(value.to_u32() / (Self::SECONDS_PER / <$from>::SECONDS_PER)) } } )* }; } impl_time_functionality! { from = [], seconds_per = 1, try_from = [ Minutes, Hours ], type = Seconds, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds ], seconds_per = 60, try_from = [ Hours ], type = Minutes, } impl_time_functionality! { from = [ Seconds, Minutes ], seconds_per = 60 * 60, try_from = [], type = Hours, } #[test] fn test() { assert_eq!(Hours::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::from(Seconds(60 * 60)), Seconds(60 * 60)); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Minutes(60)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::from(Minutes(60)), Minutes(60)); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Minutes(60)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); assert_eq!(Hours::from(Hours(1)), Hours(1)); assert_eq!(Minutes::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Minutes(60))); assert_eq!(Seconds::try_from(Hours(1)), Ok(Seconds(60 * 60))); } Sometimes the deduplication is not worth the obfuscation that it creates, but that’s a case-by-case thing. For simple types like this (and the integer types from the standard library), the benefit is clear, as it produces the obvious intended end result and ensures the APIs are all implemented uniformly.If you find yourself adding a lot of special-casing and splitting your macro into many separate macros, that might be a sign that you’ve attempted to use this pattern in a place where it’s not helpful.In those cases, it’s probably best to just write out all your traits and impls by-hand, even if it results in some duplication.

An example of this in the wild are the integer types in the Rust language itself. A really popular reason for declarative macros is to match the format! syntax from the standard library.You don’t always need to provide such a macro, sometimes you can just take impl Into and let the user format as they please. But it can make things more readable in cases where the user will always be formatting a string, or if you want formatting to be conditionally compiled-out when disabling alloc support.ExamplesTo point at the standard library again, we can look at the todo! macro. It’s simple enough that it’s just implemented right there as a declarative macro instead of being a built-in like many other macros (similar to assert_eq!, matches!, and a few others).It’s a bit of a low-hanging fruit, but the log crate has some pretty obvious examples; info!, warn!, and error!. In general, anything with a format!-like operation benefits from a declarative macro.assert!-like macros are another example of this kind of macro. You may not think too much about it, but it can be nice to provide added details about a failure for unit tests. The assert! macros all accept format arguments at the end, and you can too if you need some adapter assert! macro.macro_rules! assert_in_range { ($input:expr, $low:expr, $high:expr, $($msg:tt)*) => {{ let input = $input; let low = $low; let high = $high; assert!( input >= $low, "{}: range check failed: {input} >= {low}", format_args!($($msg)*), ); assert!( input <= $high, "{}: range check failed: {input} <= {high}", format_args!($($msg)*), ); }}; } #[test] fn example() { let number = 5; assert_in_range!(number, 50, 100, "formatted example (input={})", number); } The failure here looks like this:thread 'example' (50) panicked at src/lib.rs:22:5: formatted example (input=5): range check failed: 5 >= 50 note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

For many types, you can get away with either the struct initialization format, or using the builder pattern.#[derive(Default)] struct Example { foo: u8, bar: String, baz: bool, } // Some initialization patterns: fn struct_initialization() { let object = Example { foo: 0, bar: format!("example formatted string"), baz: false, }; } fn struct_initialization_partial() { let object = Example { bar: format!("example formatted string"), ..Example::default() }; } fn builder_pattern() { // `ExampleBuilder` type not shown for brevity. let object = ExampleBuilder::default() .with_foo(123) .with_bar(format!("example formatted string")) .finish(); } But sometimes we want a different syntax than this, for readability reasons.Often custom syntaxes are only beneficial if there’s some common, well-accepted, pre-existing format (e.g. an existing data markup language, like JSON). But occasionally a purely custom syntax can be helpful.Containers are a great example of custom initialization syntax that everyone should have some experience with.It’s true you can (and should) implement FromIterator to initialize from some sequence of elements. But this syntax can be awkward for explicit initialization that isn’t coming from some already constructed values. So for developer convenience we often create small helper macros to improve readability.Like with many things relating to macros, only add them when you’re sure they’re useful. Think about whether the pre-existing methods for initializing objects is good enough.ExamplesIt should go without saying, but the vec! macro is a really popular example of this. And soon we will have yet another version of this, with the hash_map! macro.The best example of this I can think of for object initialization is the json! macro from the serde_json crate.This is actually a good example of using declarative macros to do something non-trivial. Specifically, note that they hide the implementation details of the macro by splitting it into multiple macros, json! is the main one you call, and it redirects to another exported macro which is hidden from documentation called json_internal.Though, I will admit, json! is one of those declarative macros I think is teetering on the edge of “should have been a procedural macro”. Though, it might be hard to safely change it over at this point.

So for developer convenience we often create small helper macros to improve readability.Like with many things relating to macros, only add them when you’re sure they’re useful. Think about whether the pre-existing methods for initializing objects is good enough.ExamplesIt should go without saying, but the vec! macro is a really popular example of this. And soon we will have yet another version of this, with the hash_map! macro.The best example of this I can think of for object initialization is the json! macro from the serde_json crate.This is actually a good example of using declarative macros to do something non-trivial. Specifically, note that they hide the implementation details of the macro by splitting it into multiple macros, json! is the main one you call, and it redirects to another exported macro which is hidden from documentation called json_internal.Though, I will admit, json! is one of those declarative macros I think is teetering on the edge of “should have been a procedural macro”. Though, it might be hard to safely change it over at this point.

Containers are a great example of custom initialization syntax that everyone should have some experience with.It’s true you can (and should) implement FromIterator to initialize from some sequence of elements. But this syntax can be awkward for explicit initialization that isn’t coming from some already constructed values. So for developer convenience we often create small helper macros to improve readability.Like with many things relating to macros, only add them when you’re sure they’re useful. And soon we will have yet another version of this, with the hash_map! macro.The best example of this I can think of for object initialization is the json! macro from the serde_json crate.This is actually a good example of using declarative macros to do something non-trivial. Specifically, note that they hide the implementation details of the macro by splitting it into multiple macros, json! is the main one you call, and it redirects to another exported macro which is hidden from documentation called json_internal.Though, I will admit, json! is one of those declarative macros I think is teetering on the edge of “should have been a procedural macro”. Though, it might be hard to safely change it over at this point.

Though, I will admit, json! is one of those declarative macros I think is teetering on the edge of “should have been a procedural macro”. Though, it might be hard to safely change it over at this point.

Sometimes you find yourself writing many similar lines of code within a small set of functions.In most cases, it’s best to just change these into helper functions and let the compiler optimize things. But sometimes you’ll run into situations where you can’t do that.You need to generate a distinct type per functional configuration (e.g. not just logic or impls).You’re using it to provide the body of a function that the macro is implementing, and you can’t generalize this function body over any trait bounds.When your macro influences the surrounding control flow (break, continue, return).For optimization reasons (which you have surely bench tested).Be careful when altering control flow.It can have some utility for really simple, localized helper macros. But I tend to consider it to be an anti-pattern to export such macros. However, used very sparingly, in unique cases to assist in implementing something, it can be helpful.Honestly, I even lean away from it for crate-local macros as well. Obfuscating the control flow negatively impacts readability in my experience.ExamplesOne example where this pattern being used for optimization reasons is within the Rust standard library. The str type specializes based on string lengths for optimization reasons (specialize_for_lengths; used here).The bytes crate actually uses some macros to reduce code duplication. See the crate-local buf_get_impl macro. This is a good example of the macro providing a common implementation for a set functions. The functions that are being implemented simply invoke the macro to expand this common implementation.An example of a crate-exported macro used to produce new types can be found in the bitflags crate. In this case, it uses some custom syntax that looks kind of like regular Rust code, so it’s a good reference for how to use some different fragment specifiers (like meta or vis).Finally, probably one of the most popular control-flow-impacting macros, is anyhow’s bail! macro. As mentioned, I’m not a fan of these kinds of macros (including this one). But I want to mention it anyway, since it fits within this set of example use-cases, and likely has some popularity. (Another potential example of this is the standard library’s ready! macro for polling futures.)A really simple example of this is constructing a newtype that redirects to the underlying implementation. We may want to ensure that the types are actually distinct from one another, but we may not want to re-implement the functionality the type provides (impl_displayable_type - example usage here - is an example of this from one of my own crates, typed-ident).// A simplified form of `impl_displayable_type` to use as an example. macro_rules! impl_displayable_type { ( name=$name:ident, over=$over:ident, docs=$docs:expr, ) => { #[doc = $docs] pub struct $name($over); impl core::fmt::Display for $name { #[inline] fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result { self.0.fmt(f) } } }; } // We have some displayable types that we don't want to conflate. impl_displayable_type! { name = ObjectId, over = u64, docs = "Example documentation here", } impl_displayable_type! { name = GroupId, over = u64, docs = concat!( "`docs` is an expression so you can do things like this.\n", "\n", "Multi-line documentation, for better readability!", ), } // So now, if we have an API like this... struct Object; impl Object { pub fn object_id(&self) -> ObjectId { todo!() } pub fn group_id(&self) -> GroupId { todo!() } } // ... You can't accidentally do something like this. fn example_bad_usage_that_no_longer_compiles(object: Object) { let group_id: GroupId = object.object_id(); // Fails to compile! } It can be tempting to use declarative macros in places where a #[derive(...)] procedural macro would make more sense. Try to avoid creating such macros unless necessary.A common toy example for declarative macros is to create a function on enums so you can get static strings of the enum variant names. But this can be accomplished through a derive macro, and that feels more idiomatic to me (like IntoStaticStr from the strum crate, or - maybe better - having a custom trait to represent this).Do what you believe the end-user would find most natural. If what your macro is doing is implementing a trait - you probably ought to make it a derive macro unless you have good reason not to.We’ll talk more about derive macros when we cover procedural macros in a later article, though.

But this can be accomplished through a derive macro, and that feels more idiomatic to me (like IntoStaticStr from the strum crate, or - maybe better - having a custom trait to represent this).Do what you believe the end-user would find most natural. If what your macro is doing is implementing a trait - you probably ought to make it a derive macro unless you have good reason not to.We’ll talk more about derive macros when we cover procedural macros in a later article, though.

This is a good example of the macro providing a common implementation for a set functions. The functions that are being implemented simply invoke the macro to expand this common implementation.An example of a crate-exported macro used to produce new types can be found in the bitflags crate. In this case, it uses some custom syntax that looks kind of like regular Rust code, so it’s a good reference for how to use some different fragment specifiers (like meta or vis).Finally, probably one of the most popular control-flow-impacting macros, is anyhow’s bail! macro. As mentioned, I’m not a fan of these kinds of macros (including this one). But I want to mention it anyway, since it fits within this set of example use-cases, and likely has some popularity. (Another potential example of this is the standard library’s ready! macro for polling futures.)A really simple example of this is constructing a newtype that redirects to the underlying implementation. We may want to ensure that the types are actually distinct from one another, but we may not want to re-implement the functionality the type provides (impl_displayable_type - example usage here - is an example of this from one of my own crates, typed-ident).// A simplified form of `impl_displayable_type` to use as an example. macro_rules! impl_displayable_type { ( name=$name:ident, over=$over:ident, docs=$docs:expr, ) => { #[doc = $docs] pub struct $name($over); impl core::fmt::Display for $name { #[inline] fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result { self.0.fmt(f) } } }; } // We have some displayable types that we don't want to conflate. impl_displayable_type! { name = ObjectId, over = u64, docs = "Example documentation here", } impl_displayable_type! { name = GroupId, over = u64, docs = concat!( "`docs` is an expression so you can do things like this.\n", "\n", "Multi-line documentation, for better readability!", ), } // So now, if we have an API like this... struct Object; impl Object { pub fn object_id(&self) -> ObjectId { todo!() } pub fn group_id(&self) -> GroupId { todo!() } } // ... #9878. Mozilla leaves Solo website owners to go it alone as hosting shuts down

If you have one of these AI-generated homepages, you'd better download and save it quick

Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30.

Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names.

Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026."

Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images.

The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of.

It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will.

Mozilla told The Register: "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider."

It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere.

Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now.

Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting recursive clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know.

Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.

An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks. When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone.

The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Elijah Newren is a Staff Software Engineer at GitHub. He is the designer and implementer of merge-ort, Git's default merge strategy since 2.34, author of git-filter-repo—the history rewriting tool the Git project officially recommends—and a driving force behind sparse-checkout.

#9876. Reintroducing Spaces

Atproto Spaces are a new primitive in the atproto stack. We just launched the protocol in alpha. Check it out, give the blogpost a read, and sign up on the alpha PDS!

My own intuition around this protocol has been consistently evolving as I’ve worked on it. You can trace much of that through the Permissioned Data Diary series I wrote during the design process. Now with some time and perspective, I wanted to zoom back out, look at the design of Spaces and take a shot at succinctly motivating them as a new primitive.

Our initial goal was to extend atproto to work for non-public data. Specifically though, we wanted to enable social use cases. Which is to say that the protocol isn’t intended for just bookmarks or even “gated posts”, but needs to work for large multi-user social contexts such as a 100k user forum.

Our next goal is to maintain existing atproto intuition. Users publish records, those records are canonically stored in the user’s PDS, authority rests in the author’s DID, and applications crawl PDSes and sync data to build their own views. Succeeding in this means that many difficult questions around things like moderation and credible exit are already answered!

An extension of that goal is that it must be atmospheric. I use “atmospheric” to refer to the same underlying data getting remixed across apps in different lights. Think: Bluesky posts showing up as comments under a standard.site blog or rpg.actor characters walking across the bottom of your streamplace stream. Atmospheric features are the features that make this network feel like one deeply integrated experience rather than a bunch of isolated apps that just happen to have the same login.

And finally, the protocol needs to be secure and legible to users. This protocol enables many-to-many sharing in a multi-app, multi-pds, multi-modality network. That’s a lot of variables! This all comes to a head in the OAuth consent screen. And being able to communicate what an app is allowed to do in a concrete way in just a couple sentences is absolutely critical to the Atmosphere being broadly approachable and usable.

Spaces are our new primitive. Each space represents a shared social context. They’re a simple and concrete mechanism for organizing and permissioning data. Built around an abstraction of locality, each record is “in” a space and only one space. Each space is explicitly tied to a particular modality and owned by a single entity.

As we explored this new primitive, we realized that it seems uniquely able to thread the needle on all of our design goals.

Spaces are a deeply social primitive (fitting for a social networking protocol!). Spaces are not really about “who do I, as an individual, share this piece of content with”. Spaces are meant for establishing a shared social context. Records are in that context, and everyone with access to that context has the exact same view over it. It’s a shared common reality, and this shared sense of space allows for truly social applications.

We’ve started describing spaces as “mini atprotos” (btw if that sounds heavy duty, don’t worry spaces are actually very lightweight & low overhead). That analogy turns out to hold startlingly well. Not only does it help communicate the new primitive, but it also has the huge benefit that almost all of the really difficult questions of using the protocol for real-world social networks can be answered pretty simply: they’re the same as existing atproto! From moderation to account migration to the role of applications, intuition from public atproto maps very closely to spaces.

Spaces are quite legible. Of course this isn’t a gimme, the Atmosphere is pretty novel, and we’re all familiar with the new challenges of communicating this novel network to users. However, as I mentioned, this question of legibility comes to a head in the OAuth screen. In a context like that, describing “spaces” is much more grounded than trying to communicate ACLs or circles (as we’ll discuss in the next section).

One thing I didn’t expect when we started out designing spaces is how excited I would be for their applicability in public contexts as well. This realization partially underlies our shift in naming from “permissioned data protocol” to “atproto spaces”. This name shifts the focus from “who can see what” to locality. This new notion of locality is super handy and opens up all sorts of new options for data modeling. As a result of this locality, sync is also very lightweight and friendly. It felt so good to build my spaces example app and not have to comb through the entire global network. Locality in the sync protocol gave me exactly the data I needed.

To be upfront, the effect of designing spaces to be usable in multi-user social contexts is that they are less tailored towards permissioned publishing. Spaces are least tuned to the use case of publishing a bunch of individual pieces of content where each record has a different audience. If you realize that this seems like a weird approach to “I have a bunch of recipes and I want to share each with a totally different audience”, you’re not wrong! That use case was just not the primary design goal of atproto spaces.

That being said, I think spaces still work in that case. This deserves a blogpost & an example app of its own. However, a simple “out” for cases like this is to just put all your recipes in a space that you share with one or more applications and then let those applications manage the access logic.

In an effort to further bolster intuition around spaces, I also wanted to compare them to the most commonly-suggested alternate approach. I broadly refer to this approach as “Circles” (after Google+ Circles).

Circles: the content is the object, audience is an attribute you attach to it. You write a post, then tag it with who can see it.

Spaces: space is the object, content is published into it. A post goes "into" a space and is viewable by anyone with access to the space.

Circles come in many forms. The simplest is just “putting ACLs on records”. Once you start enabling large multi-user social use cases like forums, you realize you need to share the same ACL across many records owned by many users. Now you have a circle!

In their fullest forum, circles can be created by anyone, re-used by anyone, and apply to any data. For example, my friend can create the circle “Besties” and I can share recipes, blogposts, and videos with that circle.

However, softer versions of circles include arguments that records should be able to be in more than one space. Once you change this invariant, a record is no longer “in” a space. The record “exists” (outside of any given space), and then each space is attached as metadata, giving the record visibility in that space. We’re back to circles!

Circles seem simple at first pass, and they’re are many folks’ first instinct for social permissioning (including mine!). However they hide a lot of complexity. For one, there’s a lot of cognitive overhead, juggling who’s in which circle and which content is shared with whom. And thinking through the repercussions of sharing a post with multiple circles is difficult to understand. For instance, if I share with my “Family” and my “Besties” circles, are they able to see each other’s comments and likes?

All of this complexity gets dramatically exacerbated in the multi-app, multi-pds, multi-modality network that I described earlier.

I have a claim, which I’ll (cheekily) call Daniel’s Circles Postulate:

To quickly get the intuition behind this claim, consider that “Besties” circle from before (different account & different modality). If I upload a video with my video app and share it with Besties, my friend (who created the circle) can use his recipe app to change the access perimeter on my video. Not only does this violate all rules and intuition about resource ownership, but even if it is actually what you intend to do, I have no earthly idea how you would make those side-effects legible to either of the users involved or go about communicating that capability in the recipe app’s OAuth screen.

In short, the Atmosphere is a very dynamic network, there are a lot of variables at play. In this flux, I believe we benefit by having a deeply social, grounded, and concrete primitive that orders our interaction model. I don’t believe that any variation on circles (ACLs, the full fluid expression, or just allowing records to surface in multiple spaces) gives that to us.

So please give it a go! Check out the recent blogpost for directions on how to get started with the alpha, or just head over to the new BPS site to get your invite code for the alpha PDS.

Please let me know your thoughts! Share what you build. Let me know what works, and let me know what doesn’t. What’s confusing, what’s a pain to do, what breaks.

I can’t express enough how much I appreciate all the feedback along the way, so please keep it coming. I really believe this protocol is going to be critical for the Atmosphere, so we need to make sure it’s something we’re all excited about building on.

Let’s build the future of the internet :)

#9875. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.
