#9864. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9862. clice v1.0 Released: Welcome to Modern C++

clice recently hit 1,000 commits, a special milestone for the project. Since July 19, 2026, clice has been shipping nightly builds and going through roughly four months of alpha testing, with a huge number of bugs fixed thanks to real-world feedback from early users. Over the same stretch, I built a rigorous testing system for clice and ran extensive tests across many real open-source projects, tracking down and fixing the issues they uncovered. What does that mean? Every core feature is now stable, and you rarely run into problems in day-to-day use. So I think the time is right to ship the first stable release. The project looks very different today from where it stood two years ago in Design and Implementation of a New C++ Language Server, and this is probably the first time I’m promoting it widely, so please let me introduce it to you once again! This is the project I have poured the past two and a half years into, the work I am proudest of, the one that has excited me the most and left me sad and anxious more times than I can count, and the most ambitious thing I have taken on in my short life.

In short, clice is a C/C++ language server written in modern C++, but it’s more than just a language server. It is still built on LLVM/Clang, but unlike clangd and ccls, which are also Clang-based, clice was redesigned from the ground up to fix architectural problems that have gone unsolved in those servers for years. It is written entirely in C++23 and serves as an example of modern C++ best practices in its own right, with all the major modern C++ features coming together remarkably well:

People are always debating whether modern C++ features like modules are actually ready for real work. clice’s answer is: yes, of course, completely usable! They hold up for complex software like clice, with hundreds of thousands of lines of code. Maybe this is what the modern C++ we have been hoping for looks like. That said, the surrounding ecosystem really is inconvenient enough right now that getting this whole workflow running end to end took a huge amount of effort on my part to track issues and adapt everything.

Here is an overview of clice’s main features:

Multi-process compilation: clice compiles code in a process pool modeled after modern web browsers, whereas clangd uses multithreading. Why multiple processes? Because C++ is simply too complex, and on certain corner cases the compiler can easily crash or leak memory. That is especially true for incomplete code in the middle of editing: a huge downstream user base tests compilers on complete code, while very few people test them on half-written code, where the compiler mostly falls back on best-effort heuristics. In clangd, a compiler crash takes down the whole server and forces a restart. In clice, compilation happens in isolated child processes: losing one worker does not affect the rest of the server, so go-to-definition, highlighting, and other services keep working. It also makes it much easier to manage memory usage and schedule compilation priorities, cutting down on unnecessary resource consumption.

Modules and shared caching: clice has full support for C++20 named modules. All you need is a compile_commands.json containing all module files, and clice scans dependencies on its own and lazily builds required modules on demand, regardless of your build system or compiler, with full support for module completion, highlighting, go-to-definition, hover, and more. Built PCHs and PCMs are also cached on local disk for reuse across sessions. By comparison, clangd offers only very limited module support and no persistent cache.

Compilation context: clice has full support for non-self-contained files, and more generally for the concept of a compilation context. You can explicitly pick the active context of a file: a specific compile command for a source file, or a specific inclusion site for a header. When you open a non-self-contained file, clice detects its context automatically, so it works out of the box. More broadly, it also supports grouping compile commands into build configurations, letting you switch between, say, debug and release.

Better template support: clice implements a DFS pseudo instantiator that infers what many dependent names resolve to without needing concrete template arguments for a full instantiation. When a template has been instantiated once, clice also draws on that instantiation to power language features, such as completing on auto parameters of a lambda passed to a ranges call. On top of that, clice treats a template as a duck-typed interface and each instantiation as one of its implementations, much like a virtual function and its overrides: Go to Implementation on a dependent call inside a template lists the functions it actually calls across every instantiation, and Find References and Call Hierarchy work the same way.

Out-of-the-box experience: Most projects need nothing more than a compile_commands.json. clice ships with built-in environment probing for 50+ toolchains, covering nvcc, MSYS2, Cygwin, zigcc, and more, automatically handling mismatches between your actual compiler and Clang. You don’t have to manually add piles of compiler flags to a config file the way you do with clangd.

Beyond these main features, clice also fixes a long list of smaller clangd issues that have gone untouched for years across semantic highlighting, folding, hover, and more. If you’re interested, give it a try and see what surprises you find. Overall, clice surpasses clangd in ease of use, feature support, and performance. You can install the clice extension in VS Code and other editors and start using it right now.

Besides running as a language server, clice can also be used from the CLI to access its language features directly. Currently supported subcommands include:

That wraps up the feature tour. Next, I want to talk about the story behind the project, some of its design decisions, and my own thoughts and struggles along the way, especially now, in the age of AI.

First, why start a new project instead of improving clangd? That is the question I get asked most often. There are several reasons. I discussed some of them in my earliest post, and today those problems are even easier to see firsthand:

Maintenance and staffing: At root, clangd has been effectively unmaintained since around 2024. That sounds surprising. How could a tool used by hundreds of thousands of developers have no one maintaining it? I stumbled onto this fact in 2024 when I was getting ready to submit a PR to clangd for better code completion inside templates. From what I understand, it ties back to a shift in Google’s C++ strategy. Before that, clangd was maintained mainly by several Google engineers, and around 2024 Google started scaling back its investment in C++ (Clang); clangd was deemed good enough for Google’s internal needs, and those engineers were reassigned elsewhere. Since then, clangd has lacked any real long-term maintainers. Only Nathan Ridge has been answering questions unpaid in his spare time, purely out of passion, and one person only has so much bandwidth, making it nearly impossible to handle large PRs. That is why clangd’s C++20 modules PR dragged on for nearly a year, and even today it still isn’t really usable on large projects, with plenty of flaws and nobody working on them. Earlier this year, in 2026, Clang’s lead maintainer Aaron Ballman recognized the problem and posted a call for help on the community forum, saying clangd is very close to unmaintained, with a heavy backlog of PRs and issues, and hoping to find new community maintainers; otherwise clangd could eventually be removed from the LLVM project.

Scale of the code changes: As mentioned at the start, clice introduces many new architectural ideas, such as multi-process compilation. Implementing those inside clangd would come close to rewriting clangd. Nobody is going to review and accept changes of that size. Self-hosting with modules would also require sweeping changes to LLVM’s build system, which I will go into in detail when I introduce xclang later.

LLVM repository constraints: clice relies on a lot of third-party libraries for better performance and user experience, such as libuv, simdjson, and tomlplusplus. To keep builds simple, LLVM requires the repository to remain self-contained, so pulling in that many third-party libraries is out of the question. You would either have to rewrite and port them into LLVM or put up with worse ergonomics and lower performance. On top of that, a language server is not a standalone project: it also includes extensions and adapters for different editors. Keeping them in the same repo as the server makes maintenance much easier, and LLVM would be just as unlikely to accept that editor code (spanning Rust, Lua, TypeScript, and so on). For long-term maintainability and our core goals, a separate repository was unavoidable.

So in mid-2024, I started looking into how to design and write a new language server. At the end of 2024, I published Design and Implementation of a New C++ Language Server, setting out clice’s core goals and kicking off development in earnest.

Next, let’s talk about how clice was built. How did it get to its current state? Over the past two and a half years, at a rough guess, I have put nearly 3,000 hours into this project. Even that number doesn’t really tell the story, because clice became part of my life. It was always on my mind, like eating or sleeping: there wasn’t a moment when I wasn’t turning over some problem related to it. Development broke down into roughly four stages:

Mid-2024 to early 2025: I spent this period studying Clang and clangd’s codebase and internals. Anyone who has looked through my older blog posts will know I am a longtime template metaprogramming enthusiast, familiar with C++ and its implementation details down to language-lawyer territory. During this phase I settled on clice’s core goals and overall design, and put together an initial demo. I was a third-year undergrad at the time: I would wake up and start coding right away, skip lunch, walk out to the McDonald’s outside the campus gate when I got hungry, and put in 8 to 10 hours a day.

Early 2025 to early 2026: I originally expected to ship a usable version of clice fairly quickly during this stage. Instead, progress went much slower than I expected, and it remained a long way from production-ready. Looking back, there were a few main reasons:

Early 2026 to July 2026: The turning point came when coding agents led by Claude Opus 4.6 started catching on. I began using agents to help with the mountain of tedious detail work and painful cross-platform debugging, and found they were remarkably good at it. During this stretch I did a sweeping cleanup of the existing codebase and established the prototype of clice as it stands today. As agents grew stronger, I handed them increasingly complex tasks and kept moving the project forward rapidly. It was an exciting period: I could finally stop burning hours on tedious details and focus on architecture and feature work. At the same time, it hit me that coding agents were only going to keep getting stronger. If humans stop writing code altogether in the future, what point does a language server even have? That pushed me to start designing and building clice’s CLI features.

July 2026 to present: By July I felt the timing was right to put out early test builds and iterate based on real user feedback. Core language server features were already in place and fully usable day to day, though still short of everything I had originally envisioned, so I threw myself into building out the rest of that vision, tuning performance, and fixing bugs. In October, I started planning clice’s modular self-hosting. That was a remarkably complicated undertaking, because C++ module support today is a long, painful story:

I surveyed the options extensively, and the answer was that an out-of-the-box setup for this simply did not exist in open source, and most open-source C++ module projects don’t have build requirements nearly this involved. After thinking it through carefully, I built xclang, inspired by zigcc, to give every target platform a unified cross-compilation experience, and paired it with Bazel (which includes built-in build caching) to solve the build problem for good. Going one step further, I wrote clice modularize to automatically generate module wrappers for every third-party library we depend on, completing clice’s self-hosted modularization! That probably makes clice one of the most complex open-source C++ projects using modules today.

Alongside all of this, I ran extensive fuzz testing across many open-source projects and fixed a huge number of bugs, bringing clice to genuine production readiness!

As I mentioned earlier, I designed a CLI interface for clice so that it would still hold some value in the agent era. An obvious idea is replacing grep with clice query: it is more accurate and uses fewer tokens. That is true, except exact symbol lookup requires indexing the whole project first, which takes a very long time. grep is imprecise, sure, yet 2 or 3 grep calls are usually enough to find the target, and the extra text grep pulls back isn’t necessarily a bad thing for helping an agent understand the codebase. Put plainly, most of this CLI isn’t actually all that useful. The part that really earns its keep is probably clice modularize: if you ask an agent to modularize a project on its own, it spins up a swarm of subagents and writes custom scripts to pull off the migration, which is both slow and expensive. Giving the agent clice modularize to assist the migration works much better. LLMs are trained first and foremost for generality, and what they do best is writing and combining scripts to generalize across problems. As things stand, only highly specialized tools still carry real value; otherwise you are usually better off letting the LLM compose its own scripts.

As agents keep getting stronger, especially with models led by Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2, the cost of building complex software keeps falling, and 10x or even 100x the productivity of the past is well within reach. Over on X, you can see plenty of people asking Claude in a single sentence to rewrite the TypeScript compiler in another programming language and getting better performance out of it. Surprising at first glance, yet completely reasonable when you think about it. Software written in the past was bounded by human time, cost, and skill, so codebases inevitably accumulated lots of suboptimal code paths. When humans optimize performance, we go after the main bottlenecks, whereas an agent can tirelessly optimize every path until the small wins add up. Refactoring also often produces a better architecture than existing code; rewriting or refactoring software was just too expensive to justify before. In the foreseeable future, then, most code may be written entirely by agents, humans may stop writing code and even reading it (which is already happening now), and language servers may have no reason to exist at all. Agents might even invent programming languages better suited to themselves: compilation and interpretation themselves have often become the bottleneck in the agent loop, and agents already have the ability to optimize that underlying infrastructure; they just haven’t started yet. Ideally, every stage of the agent loop should be something the agent itself can improve and speed up, compilers and toolchains included.

That is a sad reality, and in an era like this it means the effort I poured into clice over the past two and a half years is unlikely to have the lasting meaning I first imagined. Every time I dwell on it, I slip into a dark mood, bordering on nihilism. I can’t help asking myself: thousands of hours and a lot of money, and what was it all for?

Because I taught myself programming off the beaten path without a CS degree, I got used early on to the cycle of finding my own goals, defining problems, solving them, and then looking for the next goal. Interest alone only sustains me for a little while; sticking with something for the long haul takes some deeper “meaning” or “vision” behind it, ideally one I defined for myself. And now that meaning is fading away. So over the past few months, I started pushing myself relentlessly. The more those thoughts crept in, the harder I used agents to drive the project forward, trying to finish it before it lost its meaning altogether.

Imagine an alternate timeline where coding agents never took off. clice wouldn’t be nearly as complete as it is today, of course, yet I would have slowly gained experience, learned how to collaborate and plan work, built a community around it, and watched clice move forward slowly and steadily. Except the SOTA models have already been trained. Models like Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 are real, and whether AI is a bubble or not, they aren’t going away. Software becoming cheap is already an undeniable fact.

We have to face reality, so what mindset should we bring to all of this? My thinking has shifted again recently, though honestly neither my mental state nor my daily life is in a great place right now. Pouring yourself too deeply into one thing naturally takes a heavy toll when it doesn’t turn out the way you hoped. Still, if you zoom out over a longer stretch of time, what does it really amount to? Even if I had done nothing at all for these two and a half years, so what? There is plenty of life ahead. I know that in principle, yet letting go is hard, especially when this project has been part of my life for over two years. As I mentioned in an earlier post, graduating from college never really felt real to me, because the rhythm of my life barely changed afterward: apart from my job, it was just this project. Something has to change eventually, though. I can treat clice as my graduation project: my real graduation project, not one from the chemistry major I never really liked. And that’s enough. I don’t need to force a grander meaning onto it. This graduation project has met every single goal I set two years ago, and exceeded them by a wide margin. It stands on its own as the best illustration of modern C++, neatly bringing together everything I studied about C++ in college. If on top of that it can be helpful to people just learning to program or curious about modern C++, that is plenty.

So this post is a kind of ritual for me. I need to step out of my old life and look for other things worth doing, maybe things outside code. I will keep maintaining clice, just not at the intensity I used to; practically everything worth building is already built anyway, so from here on it will mostly be incremental optimizations and bug fixes based on user feedback. In times like these, it is hard to say what the right path is, or what you ought to be doing. Nobody knows what will happen next week, let alone next year, or how far AI will actually go. I think it is time to rest for a while so I don’t burn out, and have the energy to face whatever problems come next. I still have a strong drive to keep creating good work. It just might not be about programming anymore, and figuring that out is what I need to learn and think through in this next stage.

That’s all for this post. Thanks for reading. I hope you’ll give clice a try, and feel free to report any problems!

#9861. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9860. FAA blames ground stop on faulty copper wiring

Safety reasons and unspecified communications issue cited

The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevented the takeoff of flights in US airspace for around five hours, creating chaos for travelers and airports. The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded.

In a press conference Saturday, Transportation Secretary Duffy attributed the FAA ground stop to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade. Duffy said it has yet to be determined whether the issue was incompetence or a faulty router.

In a statement provided to The Register on Saturday, a spokesperson for L3Harris said, “L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

The stop was issued on Friday around the middle of the day ET.

"The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement on Friday. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them."

A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone at the time said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement.

The FAA ATCSCC advisory halted departing flights and said international flights would be dealt with individually.

The notice said, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis."

Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now."

An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage."

The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. ®

Updated at 0039 UTC Sunday UTC with the administration's explanation for the stop.

Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop.

CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.”

Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

#9858. Anthropomorphic Software

There are some programs that I like to call anthropomorphic software. These programs have copy in the first person that is personified. A distinction I would like to make is that LLMs and other conversational AI do not count. I will, however, talk about them at the end.

A familiar example is Git. Have you ever tried to create a commit on a freshly installed system? You might have encountered this error:

Quite personal for a tool whose primary use is to track mistakes.

Start a rebase while Git finds an existing rebase in progress. It also says "run me again" and "I am stopping."

In an interactive terminal, mark a revision during bisect before starting the bisect.

My favourite. During git bisect, skip enough commits that Git cannot narrow the answer further.

Adjacently, Git changelogs too are personified:

"git fsck" learned to catch NUL byte in a commit object as potential error and warn.

CI test was taught to build documentation pages.

The Elm programming language is an extreme example.

I like this effect when used sparingly, unlike Elm.

With this option enabled, sudo will insult you if you enter an incorrect password:

If you have ever attempted Linux From Scratch, you will know that Bash can say "I have no name!" in the prompt.

On September 1, running Nmap with -v makes it wish itself happy birthday.

It also wishes users a merry Christmas on December 25.

If you are aware of any more examples, I would be glad to list them here.

LLM agents are the ultimate version of anthropomorphic software. But agents do not have to sound human. I force my agents to not speak like humans for my own sanity. Agents might become the default paradigm of computer user interface in the future. I will miss anthropomorphic software then.

Most usage of this effect is purely for whimsy and isn't intended to improve the user experience. Apple's user interface guidelines prescribe avoiding error messages that contain "uh-oh!"s and "oops"es.

#9857. Please Implement A Quorum Database

Posted 2026-11-1518 minute reading timeMandatory Legal Disclaimer:Opinions expressed are solelymy own and do not express theviews or opinions of my employer.

I return with part two of the replication rants series. This talk was given at HPTS'26 and fleshes out the argument for quorum-based replication in Enough With All The Raft, and continues to build off of the work that went into writing Data Replication Design Spectrum.

I think we tend to view quorum replication as generally impractical for production use.

If you want the links to papers, find the corresponding slide below.

This is a replication talk that I gave at HPTS 2026.

I once did a survey of what type of replication algorithm databases in production are using, and the result looks like this. Raft is the giant pacman, eating the primary-backup and quorum slices. The Quorum slice is small enough that we can just fully enumerate it right now.

Upper left are OSS majority quorum databases. Upper right are proprietary ones that used or are using it for data replication. Bottom left are proprietary ones using consensus for a log. Bottom right are technically true but carry caveats.

If we filter that list by how they’re doing now:

Voldemort is so dead all that all of you forgot it existed until the previous slide.

InfluxDB and Grafana Mimir had previous iterations which used quorums, and then they re-architected.

Weviate does quorum for data and raft for metadata, and I won’t be shocked if they re-architected too.

Tencent PaxosStore is super internal in chinese bigtech, so I have no idea.

CouchDB was more meant for eventual consistency but has a clustered mode, and I have no idea who uses it other than cloudant?

OG Dynamo, which someone here can tell me about, but I’m assuming is/has been phased out?

Note: the HPTS audience head shaking agreed with my assessment of Dynamo.

Which leaves me with this awkward feeling that if I say implement a quorum database, the only good example I have to point to is Cassandra?!?

HPTS says submit your spicy takes, so brace yourself: I think we should be credibly building more than one good example of a quorum database.

Which we are! I’m holding out 3 very recent examples on you.

But first, for the next 16 minutes I will be CEO and utterly delusional founder of CashDB, because I need a running example for this talk. CashDB is a database specialized for whatever your splitting-the-bill-with-friends app that you use.

First, it only supports a very limited set of operations:

The second constraint is that I told a coding agent to make CashDB as reliable as possible and now it has my AWS keys, is rebooting one of my VMs once a minute in the name of chaos testing, and has replicated itself. I cannot stop it. We must now design CashDB around this. I need a replicated CashDB.

If I use a reconfiguration-based replication protocol that does a view change on every failure, my users are going to see latency spikes every minute and I will have to answer uncomfortable questions.

If I use raft, then expected value is that they see a latency spike every five minutes when the leader is affected, but the other failures get masked.

This is the motivation I’m pitching for being leaderless. You should get better latency,

I’m not saying availability, because availability is just a latency SLO.

So, what if we try to build CashDB in the style of our long-established examples?

First we have everything that came out of the ABD paper doing standard majority quorums.

Hagit Attiya, Amotz Bar-Noy, and Danny Dolev. 1995. Sharing memory robustly in message-passing systems. Journal of the ACM 42, 1 (January 1995), 124–142. [scholar]

Think OG cassandra. We get a nice 1 or 2 RTT writes. We get 1-2 RTT reads. Life is great.

It implements only distributed read/write register, thus the implicit atomic read-modify-write for account debit/credit operations doesn’t work. Append to transaction log would also be a struggle.

I think we view majority quorums slightly worse than it deserves because it came from the eventual consistency era read repair + LWW + anti-entropy gives a lot of opportunities to resurrect failed writes.

But, unless you very knowingly fit the register model with linearizable-but-sujectively-worse consistency, I do not think majority quorums are the path forward.

Let us instead consider if building a system like Megastore would work.

Jason Baker, Chris Bond, James C. Corbett, JJ Furman, Andrey Khorlin, James Larson, Jean-Michel Leon, Yawei Li, Alexander Lloyd, and Vadim Yushprakh. 2011. Megastore: Providing Scalable, Highly Available Storage for Interactive Services. In Proceedings of the Conference on Innovative Data system Research (CIDR), 223–234. [scholar]

Megastore replicates a log per entity group, and a proposer targets the next available slot in the log with its proposal. This is just multi-paxos without the time-based leader election. Consensus gives us State Machine Replication, and thus we can model debits and credits as increments and decrements, and log appends as appends. That’s great.

It will fail because of latency. Paxos has a liveness problem: two duelling proposers can easily prevent eachothers' progress. The log-centric model only helps to funnel proposers into conflict.

Megastore optimization: if you commit to slot N, you’re automatically the "leader" for slot N+1.

PaxosStore: time-based exclusion for a log slot once you hear a proposal for it (also geographic closeness).

However, it’s nice that replica catchup is easy because there’s one log with one ordering to replicate, and one can easily describe a snapshot of data by just the log offset. But, the latency spikes worse than leader election timeouts removes the motivation for using quorums in the first place.

What if we built CashDB using some E-Paxos ideas?

Iulian Moraru, David G. Andersen, and Michael Kaminsky. 2013. There is more consensus in Egalitarian parliaments. In Proceedings of the Twenty-Fourth ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '13), ACM, 358–372. [scholar]

Egalitarian Paxos introduces doing consensus where one agrees upon an order only for the exactly necessary dependencies. This naively results in a sparse, potentially disconnected, graph of operations. This graph frees us from having the One Big Log causing unnecessary contention. The closest that E-Paxos gives to any hint on how to do replica catchup is something that looks very much like Cassandra Enhancement Proposal 45 Mutation Tracking if you squint at it.

Our almost production example comes from Cassandra again. There’s an old 50k line un-merged patch which gives Lightweight Transactions an overhaul onto a new E-Paxos implementation.

It’s not clearly better or worse than a log here…​

E-Paxos also was noted to have a huge latency cliff under contention, which again ruins our latency desires. There’s actually an infinite tail latency theoretical result for this.

E-Paxos doesn’t give any great way to define a snapshot other than commit a dependency on everything.

Cassandra’s EPaxos already had anti-entropy and so they had a paxos repair that ran every 5min to fix up lost proposals. It still benchmarked better than LWT though.

For things that have a good history in production, that’s it. It doesn’t seem great.

From looking at what pieces were good and bad, we can put together the missing feature wishlist for leaderless replication:

We need to survive contention because we cannot have latency climb incredulously as contention increases. We desire quorums for low latency. If there’s an easy trap that causes concerningly high latency, then we might as well use Raft.

Consistent local snapshots would be nice. If you need to do a quorum read and merge for a table scan while executing SQL, you’re going to lose tremendously to a system which doesn’t. We need some way to define a consistent snapshot locally.

Lastly, If a node has missed proposals, catching up (to get to a snapshot) should be O(missed work) and not O(total data).

So let’s do another pass, and now look at some very recent approaches instead.

If we look back at consensus over logs, the thing we need to fix is the latency under contention. How can we do that?

SOSP'23 had a paper on QuePaxa. QuePaxa gives us leaderless consensus that offers much better bounded latency under contention. Proposers collaborate instead of conflict. Consensus will take somewhere from 1 to 7RTT. But you’re unlikely to go over 7RTT.

Pasindu Tennage, Cristina Basescu, Lefteris Kokoris-Kogias, Ewa Syta, Philipp Jovanovic, Vero Estrada-Galinanes, and Bryan Ford. 2023. QuePaxa: Escaping the tyranny of timeouts in consensus. In Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '23), ACM, 281–297. DOI:https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613150 [scholar]

Every proposal gets a priority value, priority equals value for sake of diagram simplicity.

The algorithm proceeds with proposers walking in lockstep through phases across the acceptors.

If you fall off the lockstep bandwagon, you can get back on with some other valid proposer’s state.

Phase 1 only records the first proposal it hears.

From then on there is a fixed number of proposals, and the consensus intuition is:

I define a phase as "read from a quorum of phase N and write the max priority proposal to a quorum to begin phase N+1", if I repeat that enough times, everyone should eventually become aware of the best proposal.

You can replace paxos in a megastore-style system with QuePaxa.

QuePaxa’s 1RTT fastpath comes from a spiritually similar Megastore optimization where winning round N gives you an ability to do a 1RTT commit to round N+1.

I’m nearly certain some of those 7RTT cases can be trimmed down. Superficially, pipelining isn’t discussed, and so getting good throughput seems hard. QuePaxa needs like 5 more optimization papers, and then it’s very worth revisiting.

Note: I had received a question about the jump from E-Paxos to QuePaxa, and what QuePaxa was trying to solve. The intended comparison is mostly just Megastore to QuePaxa, and I think the chance of you regretting putting Megastore into production is much higher than the chance of you regretting putting QuePaxa (+ Optimizations) into production.

Cloudflare is working on pushing QuePaxa into production, and so I hope they’ll also do a lot of that needed optimization work. I highly look forward to their results.

If we look back at consensus over graphs, we need to fix…​ everything. Which sounds hard, but we actually have two great examples here.

SIGMOD'26 gave us Neo4J doing a very graph-centric leaderless consensus protocol.

Jim Webber, Georgios Theodorakis, Hugo Firth, and Natacha Crooks. 2026. RIOT: Replicated Independently-Ordered Transactions. In Companion of the International Conference on Management of Data (SIGMOD Companion '26), Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 464–476. [scholar]

Note: Jim Webber was at HPTS'26 and came up to say hello after this talk. He is a very nice person, and it was really cool to get to meet him.

RIOT builds a DAG where each transaction is a node, and the current snapshot is defined as the set of nodes with no parents, the “Leading Edge”. Nodes gain a dependency when they conflict, or have a time ordering.

Add yourself as a node with the snapshot as your parents. You are now the leading edge.

Each node becomes a new part of the "leading edge".

And RIOT is centered around the leading edge. Transactions are committed when a quorum accepts a new node into the transaction graph, and that’s sent with a leading edge. If you hear about a node you don’t know about from another replica, you get caught up on it, and all its parents you don’t know about. RIOT tells us you can do DAG replication by keeping our DAGs connected, and keep them tall and narrow.

Their results show…​ it’s like, pretty okay at low-ish concurrency: 300txn/partition/second. And that’s fine for neo4j usage, and they have production stats that justify that the tradeoffs in RIOT match their production usage well, which is really all I want to see when picking a replication algorithm.

It’s just not an amazing fit for CashDB. CashDB would do lots of small transactions. RIOT happens better for fewer and larger transactions. It’s a super cool paper either way. it’s the only thing I’ve seen that answers how to do pure DAG replication like this well, and it gave Neo4J lower latency than their Raft implementation.

Our second system to examine is, you won’t believe it, but it’s Cassandra again, because we can’t stop talking about Cassandra in every part of this talk. CEP-15 introduces Accord, which is an E-Paxos style protocol.

Benedict Elliott Smith, Tony Zhang, Blake Eggleston, and Scott Andreas. 2021. CEP-15: Fast general purpose transactions. Retrieved from https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/CASSANDRA/pages/188744725/CEP-15+General+Purpose+Transactions

Its closest direct relative is the tempo paper, but accord does physical timestamps instead of logical timestamps.

Vitor Enes, Carlos Baquero, Alexey Gotsman, and Pierre Sutra. 2021. Efficient replication via timestamp stability. In Proceedings of the Sixteenth European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys '21), ACM, 178–193. [scholar]

Accord provides a 1RTT fast path. It takes up to 3RTT in the slowest case. It borrows the ordered broadcast optimization from E-Paxos Revisited, which means you’ll end up on the fast path more often

It collects agreement on what timestamp to execute a transaction at, such that the timestamp is after all of its dependencies. The same epaxos-like logic applies for dependency collection, but, the reliance on the timestamp stability work dodges the e-paxos infinite tail latency theoretical result.

Timestamp ordered execution linearizes proposals which gives it an easy way to support consistent local snapshots and incremental replica catch-up.

CashDB would be only small OLTP transactions. It doesn’t need interactivity. You would have to commit a debit/credit, and then execute it and find out if it was valid or not as like a durable OCC, but that’s not the worst.

I like Accord a lot and think you should read about it.

And I wanted to take an extra quick moment to highlight that epaxos revisited ordered broadcast primitive.

The difficult part of leaderless consensus is agreeing upon ordering. Leaders are great at ordering! Wouldn’t it be great if everything could just be ordered upon arrival?

Client generated timestamps. Make up your order on your client, broadcast it with your message. Variants of this idea show up in papers often.

What if you process messages only on or after their deadline?

Sarah Tollman, Seo Jin Park, and John Ousterhout. 2021. EPaxos Revisited. In 18th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 21), USENIX Association, 613–632. [scholar]

What if you also drop out-of-order messages?

Jinkun Geng, Anirudh Sivaraman, Balaji Prabhakar, and Mendel Rosenblum. 2022. Nezha: Deployable and High-Performance Consensus Using Synchronized Clocks. Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 16, 4 (December 2022), 629–642. [scholar]

What if the network provides best effort ordering?

Dan R. K. Ports, Jialin Li, Vincent Liu, Naveen Kr. Sharma, and Arvind Krishnamurthy. 2015. Designing Distributed Systems Using Approximate Synchrony in Data Center Networks. In 12th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 15), USENIX Association, Oakland, CA, 43–57. [scholar]

Rida Bazzi and Maurice Herlihy. 2022. Clairvoyant state machine replication. Information and Computation 285, (May 2022), 104701. [scholar]

No details for time, and we’re ending on TAPIR so I can mention System #3 that I think SurrealDB is putting TAPIR into production which is pretty cool.

Irene Zhang, Naveen Kr. Sharma, Adriana Szekeres, Arvind Krishnamurthy, and Dan R. K. Ports. 2017. Building Consistent Transactions with Inconsistent Replication. ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 35, 4 (November 2017), 1–37. [scholar]

Our last bag of tricks are a few very related ideas because applying any one of them, gives you the same high level architecture.

There’s a cloud of unordered commutative operations from which you pull a log out of afterwards with some great-at-ordering leadered consensus. You can do a 1RTT quorum write into the unordered pool, and remember that Linearizable Quorum Reads says you can do a 1RTT read from a quorum of non-leaders, so you’re left only stalling read-after-writes.

CURP is a really nice introduction to this idea, and hides a description of how to apply it to raft in the appendix

Seo Jin Park and John Ousterhout. 2019. Exploiting Commutativity For Practical Fast Replication. In 16th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 19), USENIX Association, Boston, MA, 47–64. [scholar]

It was then later generalized to work on more consensus algorithms and fixed in Jetpack

Ze Tang, Zihao Zhang, Weihai Shen, Jicheng Shi, and Shuai Mu. 2026. Jetpack: Consensus Made Generally Fast. In 20th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 26), USENIX Association, Seattle, WA, 1299–1323. [scholar]

Both stop at defining “commutative” operations as those that affect two different keys. Pulling this diagram from CURP, they accepted a quorum write to Y and to Z, but another write to Y would be forced to stall while the leader works on propagating Y into the log.

CURP almost got a production implementation in {uri-cncn-xline}[CNCF Xline], but they went straight from Beta to Archived.

To take these ideas one step further, you need the Skyros paper introducing Nil-Externality.

Aishwarya Ganesan, Ramnatthan Alagappan, Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, and Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau. 2021. Exploiting Nil-Externality for Fast Replicated Storage. In Proceedings of the ACM SIGOPS 28th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '21), ACM, 440–456. [scholar]

Nil-externality is a generalization of blind writes to all operations that don’t return any state about the system. Skyros lets you just keep quorum writing nil-external operations to the same key. Each replica remembers its local order, and a leadered consensus can pull back out a correct linearizable order later.

Nil-Externality has no direct implementation in industry, but we’ve been doing similar logic on the concurrency control side by not checking conflicts between blind writes in serializable MVCC databases for a long time.

Skyros tacks on commutative operations like increments but doesn’t discuss it much.

I’ll give MDCC credit as the other paper I know of which directly took on commutative updates under a leaderless generalized paxos model

Tim Kraska, Gene Pang, Michael J. Franklin, Samuel Madden, and Alan Fekete. 2013. MDCC: multi-data center consistency. In Proceedings of the 8th ACM European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys '13), ACM, 113–126. DOI:https://doi.org/10.1145/2465351.2465363 [scholar]

and 1986 Escrow transactions let you extend that commutative logic to …​ almost commutative operations.

Patrick E. O’Neil. 1986. The Escrow transactional method. ACM Transactions on Database Systems 11, 4 (December 1986), 405–430. [scholar]

Escrow says: let increments and decrements commute as long as it’s impossible for your constraint to be violated. If in the absolute worst case where all the increments abort, and all decrements succeed, then the value still remains above 0, then what do you care just treat them all as commutative.

Escrow has only one implementation I’m aware of, Oracle 23c introduced it under the name “lockfree reservations”, but, Oracle is not a quorum database

To apply this to quorum systems, you need the 1992 paper: High Throughput Escrow Algorithms for Replicated Databases which tells you that in the standard 3 of 5 quorum setup, the worst case value needs to stay above 40% of the current account value instead of 0. It’s not a terribly hard fix.

Narayanan Krishnakumar and Arthur J. Bernstein. 1992. High Throughput Escrow Algorithms for Replicated Databases. In Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Very Large Data Bases (VLDB '92), Morgan Kaufmann Publishers Inc., San Francisco, CA, USA, 175–186. [scholar]

So if we squish all these ideas together…​

CashDB only supports an escrow-able account transfer operation and a nil-external log append. I obviously designed CashDB for this argument. In isolation this async leader trick is not 100% leaderless, but I include it because it’s a great step towards better latency.

I’m also mentioning it because leveraging blind and commutative operations makes EVERY OTHER ALGORITHM BETTER and we never do it. In Consensus over Logs, Nil-Externality and Escrow would help guide us as to what operations are safe to pipeline with a leaderless log. In Consensus over Graphs, it means we get to reduce the dependencies tracked, and thus end up on the fast path more often.

Increments are the best operation ever because you can treat them as commutative OR a nil-external fused together read-modify-write that returns nothing, and we still basically never special case them?!? We just execute them under exclusive locks, it saddens me.

Alright, I’m out of time and out of content, so:

We have very recently gotten much better algorithms for leaderless replication

We have very recently gotten much better production-or-almost-there examples of how to write good quorum databases.

There are still more good ideas we have yet to apply to their full extent.

I do not think we will see a proliferation of quorum databases until we have good production examples to copy from.

So I implore you. Choose something different. Choose something with better latency. Choose something that lets you drop a "why quorums are better" blog post every time your competitor has an outage.

See discussion of this page on Reddit, Hacker News, and Lobsters.

#9856. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines)

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines)

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#9855. Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum

Accessing banned content is as easy as whipping out a thesaurus, Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee hears

Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say.

A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters.

Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms.

"Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said.

"I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable.

"So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently."

McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not.

"If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added.

Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too.

Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal.

She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly.

There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs.

"So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content."

Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories.

With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process.

As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially.

Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent.

Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures.

The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly.

Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limbo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests.

Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report, it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny.

Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment.

The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force.

England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves.

Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms.

She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.'

"In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered.

"So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®
