#9735. November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

Microsoft serves up an actively exploited Outlook zero-day, and a wave of critical Exchange, SharePoint, Windows Search, and LDAP bugs that exhausted defenders need to prioritize fast.

November offers up a veritable Patch Tuesday feast of vulnerabilities that are more likely to be exploited. In its second four-digit Patch Tuesday release in a row, Microsoft today addressed 1,093 security vulnerabilities, with 63 rated critical, and one zero-day in the mix (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS 6.5) that Microsoft confirmed is under active exploit.

"Most security teams haven't quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," says Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at Watchtowr.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out what actually matters when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention," he adds. "Our advice hasn't changed … start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what's already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."

Related:OnlyFans Copyright Takedowns Expose Compromised Websites

To that end, security teams should prioritize CVE-2026-124194, and not just because attackers are already targeting it. It's a spoofing vulnerability in Outlook that may not allow code execution, hence its moderate severity rating, but could allow the disclosure of an account’s NTLMv2 hash — and in turn, the target's login.

"To exploit it, an attacker sends a target a malicious Office file and convinces them to open it," explained Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, in his monthly Patch Tuesday commentary. "If the attack succeeds, the attacker captures the victim's NT LAN Manager v2 (NTLMv2) hash, a value derived from their Windows password. The attacker may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password."

Security teams should also prioritize a pair of critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, in Exchange and SharePoint, respectively, that each open targets to any attacker with a low-privilege login.

The first, in Exchange Server (CVE-2026-118207, CVSS 8.8), "belongs in this week's emergency window for every Exchange Server Subscription Edition server you run," Automox researchers warned in their monthly Patch Tuesday bulletin, and "all an attacker needs to start is a low-level login."

It's an improper input validation that could allow an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send the server a specially crafted request and run code with no user interaction.

Related:The Evolving Cybersecurity Lexicon: Vulnerability Discovery to Resilience

"Code on an Exchange server reaches every mailbox it hosts," warned Automox researchers. "And Exchange usually holds broad rights in Active Directory, so the mailboxes are just the start."

Meanwhile, an important-rated flaw (CVE-2026-120002, CVSS 9.9) in SharePoint Server is an elevation of privilege vulnerability that needs quick addressing, according to Automox.

"The flaw is incorrect authorization," the researchers noted. "That 9.9 comes from a changed scope: a successful attack reaches past the vulnerable SharePoint component itself. An attacker who already holds a low-privileged account sends requests over the network and elevates their privileges, with no user interaction required."

Another critical RCE to watch out for, according to Automox, is CVE-2026-110043 (CVSS 8.8/10), a one-click heap-based buffer overflow in Outlook that uses the Preview Pane as an attack vector. A target must select a weaponized email so it displays in the Preview Pane for it to trigger the attacker's code, which runs with that user's permissions.

"Patch internet-facing Exchange and SharePoint servers, and book the Exchange restart now," the Automox researchers advised. "Push the Office update this week, then check the installed build, because a fully patched Windows dashboard says nothing about Office. Rank by score and assessment, not label."

Related:Ivanti ICS Zero-Day Attacks Highlight Vendor Patching Hurdles

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), also identified a Windows Search RCE (CVE-2026-116928, CVSS 9.8) as needing immediate attention.

"We start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server," he said in his November Patch Tuesday blog post, where he also listed 30 potentially wormable CVEs to patch quickly. "This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month."

And finally, Childs pointed to CVE-2026-119958, an RCE bug in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

"This patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction," he warned. "Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly."

Childs also recommended testing and deploying patches for the wormable bugs quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange.

While the cornucopia of CVEs this month, especially on the heels of the record October Patch Tuesday, may feel overwhelming, security teams should stick to best practices and not get overwhelmed, advises Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra.

"I don't know about everyone else, but I'm tired," he says via email, adding that he believes that, eventually, AI will finish turning up old bugs and teams can once again look forward to smaller Patch Tuesday releases. "I can only imagine that if I’m tired, admins and operations teams everywhere are also tired. I believe that we will make it through to the other side, if we prioritize updates and focus on what really matters. The noise is coming at us from all sides, and we need to cut through it and figure out what really matters to the business."

InfoQ Homepage News Uber's Secure AI Framework Governs Autonomous AI Agents Across Their Lifecycle

Nov 15, 2026 3 min read

In a recent article, Uber Engineering highlights the limitations of traditional identity and API controls in securing AI agents that dynamically reason over external content and take real-world actions. To address this challenge, Uber developed a framework to determine whether an agent's action is appropriate given the user's request, the agent's intended purpose, its permissions, and the context of the interaction.

Identity and authorization systems can determine whether a user or service has permission to access a resource, but they can't determine whether an agent's proposed action is appropriate in context.

This creates multiple risks, including prompt injection, tool and memory poisoning, goal hijacking, behavioral drift, and hallucination-driven actions, which Uber's framework addresses through three layers spanning the entire agent lifecycle, from pre-deployment to runtime enforcement to post-deployment continuous assurance.

At provisioning time, agents must be registered in the Uber AI Registry, establishing identity, ownership, persona, permitted intents, constraints, dependencies, and risk classification. This process is automated using Argus, which analyzes the agent's source code, prompts, configurations, dependencies, exposed endpoints, and tool-invocation paths to identify security weaknesses. The same approach is enforced for MCP servers and tools used by the agents.

At runtime, the framework extends the traditional security model based on policy administration, policy decision, and policy enforcement to incorporate behavioral authorization, which evaluates whether an agent's actions are appropriate in a given context.

Behavioral authorization is implemented through three components: the AI Registry, AI guards, and Agent Guard runtime hooks. The AI Registry defines and manages agent policies, personas, intents, and constraints, while AI Guards evaluate interactions and proposed actions against established policies. Agent Guard runtime hooks invoke AI Guard "at critical checkpoints and applying its verdict before an interaction or action is allowed to proceed".

After deployment, the focus shifts to Continuous Assurance, which relies on end-to-end observability, auditing, explainability, and replay. This layer comprises two main main components: a unified execution trace that connects agent actions, tool calls, and security decisions; and recorded interactions that can be replayed whenever policies and guardrails are updated to assess their effectiveness in the new context.

Uber also identified several challenges in implementing security controls in production, including balancing policy restrictiveness to avoid both excessive false positives and insufficient protection, minimizing runtime latency, reducing developer friction during framework setup, and moving beyond generic controls towards agent-specific policies, which "made enforcement more contextual and precise".

Commenting on Uber's approach on LinkedIn, UN senior information technology officer Tristan G. raised several concerns, noting that while "per-agent personas, intents, constraints and calibration" is what adds the most value, they also come at a significant cost, as "the effort scales with the number of workflows". Additionally,

By its own account, the strongest control was restricting agents to explicit constraints, which is least privilege rather than a new idea. For me, the open question is how this works for agents you don't build, such as vendor or SaaS agents where you can't insert your own enforcement hooks.

On similar lines, AI architect Pratik Dhanave also observes that:

The lesson they call least glamorous is the one they rate most effective: explicit intents and constraints per agent. Not generic thresholds, which failed because every agent has a different purpose and risk profile. The cost is flexibility, and they say it is worth paying.

Uber's Secure AI framework is still in evolving, with plans to expand its capabilities across all the areas outlined above. There is much more to the framework than can be covered here, so readers are encouraged to consult the ⁠original article for a more comprehensive overview.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9731. N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws

The RMM provider also released a hotfix as a recommended mitigation to address public exploits for the alleged zero-days, which allow for attacker takeover.

N-able is navigating a hectic crisis-management situation after the discovery of more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, as well as the disclosure of exploits allowing attackers to execute commands, create administrator accounts, and escalate privileges to root.

Realizing the critical security nature of the situation, N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific after offensive security researcher Sean Bales on Sunday publicly revealed the flaws, collectively called Able2Shell, and subsequently published a series of exploits for them on the GitHub account "Oracle-Security." N-able also advised customers operating on-premises servers to shut them down until further notice.

"N-able sincerely appreciates the patience, flexibility, and partnership our customers have demonstrated throughout this critical security event," the company wrote in a security update Wednesday.

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

The extraordinary scenario has major repercussions for the entire endpoint management industry, including managed service providers (MSPs) and IT managers who broadly use N-central to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The risk for users of vulnerable platforms is significant because of the "extraordinary privileges" these RMM platforms have "because they need them to do their jobs," observes Gene Moody, field chief technology officer (CTO) for autonomous endpoint management provider Action 1.

N-able and other RMM platforms can engage in critical tasks such as script execution, software deployment, and remote administration, often across many thousands of endpoints, Moody says. The downside? "That also makes them incredibly attractive targets," he says.

Indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers are already scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security update Wednesday. The company moved fast to remedy some of the most critical flaws, releasing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on Tuesday to address seven CVEs associated with them; the company says it also plans to release further security updates.

Flaws covered by the N-able hotfix are tracked as the following: CVE-2026-125883, which covers multiple XXE vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125878, which covers multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125879, a local privilege escalation flaw; CVE-2026-125880, described as stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata; and CVE-2026-125881, a schema validation flaw.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

The patch also addresses CVE-2026-125882, which enables remote code execution (RCE) via file repository upload path traversal and was discovered by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security; and CVE-2026-91000, which leads to local privilege escalation via insecure IPC Channels.

Though Bales disclosed 33 separate flaws, some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list, according to a report from Tenable's Research Special Operations published today. All in all, Bales listed four exploit chains, with the XXE chain emerging as potentially the most significant of the issues, according to Tenable.

"The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required," the Tenable team wrote. That chain exploits an unauthenticated XXE flaw in N-central's service-import functionality and can ultimately turn an unauthenticated network request into a complete compromise of a central IT management system.

Indeed, the CyberSec Guru called the credential-free XXE exploit the "centerpiece of the release" and went into detail about how it can be exploited to create an attacker entry point into a system in a blog post updated Tuesday.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Moreover, once an attacker has compromised a platform, the other vulnerabilities can help expand their access to take over privileged internal sessions and ultimately execute commands on the underlying server, paving the way for cross-customer compromise, according to the post. This scenario is especially concerning for MSPs managing infrastructure on behalf of many organizations.

The recently disclosed flaws are not N-central's first time dealing with a significant security incident. In August 2025, CISA added two N-central vulnerabilities, CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after they were exploited in the wild.

More recently, in August 2026, attackers exploited an authentication-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-18556), subsequently finding a way around N-able's initial fix through a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-18577. The second incident allowed attackers to gain administrative access to vulnerable N-central servers and use the platform's Take Control feature to access managed systems.

The recurrence of vulnerabilities in the same management platform raises broader questions about the security of RMM infrastructure, particularly given the extensive access these tools provide to MSPs and their customers, Moody says.

"I see this as yet another warning in a recent wave of attacks on these platforms; how much authority endpoint management platforms concentrate," he says. "They are essential, but MFA and role-based access cannot contain every platform compromise."

All in all, the situation has created a significant security quagmire for N-able and its customers, who — given that exploitation of the flaws could be imminent — are advised to apply the hotfix where necessary as well as take other immediate mitigation steps.

"The clock is ticking for anyone not taking this seriously," Moody observes, advising that any affected organization "keep on-premises N-central offline until N-able provides safe restoration instructions," while preserving logs before making any changes.

Moreover, they should "review authentication and administration since at least the beginning of November, just because this is exposed does not mean it was not leveraged prior to disclosure," he warns.

Researchers from Huntress also advised organizations affected to review login and authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, according to a blog post published Monday. If they find it, they should involve incident response, as it could indicate that an attacker conducted RCE or privilege escalation on the server.

Huntress also advised organizations to examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise — such as anomalous remote access sessions or new scripts being deployed — since as during previous N-central exploitations, "threat actors were observed 'spraying' downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools."

Noting that CISA's March guidance called for least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA and second-administrator approval, Moody says he would go even further this time to protect N-able environments by keeping critical secrets and signing keys outside the platform, and making endpoints independently verify cryptographically signed approval for high-impact operations.

"Stealing a credential, or even controlling the console, should not automatically confer that authority," he says. "A login should no longer be considered enough to authorize protected operations."

During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9728. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9726. As Test Takers Turn to AI for Answers, Exam Security Must Catch Up

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

It's hard to detect whether someone is using artificial intelligence (AI) to cheat on IT certification exams, but new tools and processes are emerging to boost trust.

Certifications play a critical role in keeping up with the latest industry metamorphosis, but artificial intelligence (AI) is now muddying the verification process.

From Meta Glasses to AI browsers and deepfakes, exam administrators face a growing list of risks to monitor — and organizations need to know that the person they hired can actually do what their certification says they can.

Score legitimacy has become harder to assess as test takers use AI to fill in the blanks. As a result, the industry is shifting toward more in-person testing and stricter fraud-detection protocols to keep certifications credible.

Certifications range from entry-level cloud and cybersecurity knowledge and cover Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services updates. In some industries, like government, banking, and financial services, certified IT departments are required to stay current on compliance regulations.

Cheating is a risk that has existed for as long as testing has. But AI has significantly changed the testing game for IT certification, explains Marielle Carlos, data forensics scientist at Caveon.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Traditional threats, like harvesting pre-knowledge, plagiarism, or collusion proxy testing, have evolved as people use AI as an unauthorized aid, she says, and it has become an incredibly challenging problem.

However, the problem is still in its infancy stage — so much so that Caveon added a new category to its testing security threats taxonomy: unknown.

"It makes it hard to know if your exam is measuring actual competence or if it's measuring someone's ability to use AI to answer the question," Carlos tells Dark Reading. "It really challenges the usefulness of that exam."

Carlos spends her day interpreting test results to help programs decide whether anomalies warrant any additional attention or professional review. Over the past two years, she has seen how AI has changed the way certification programs monitor metrics to assess cheating. Previously, it may have been enough to look at speed and score separately to flag a case for review. Now attention has shifted, as administrators take numerous variables into account since AI can combine multiple cheating tactics.

During her research, Carlos noted a "huge boom of people" who are testing fast and receiving high scores. No concrete data exists that says it's all due to AI, but there is enough organizational interest and concern over that trend's growth that Carlos says she and her team will look at it more.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

But uncertainty hasn't stopped other organizations from taking action. Widespread irregular exam results and verified cheating attempts discovered during ISC2's online proctoring pilots led the nonprofit to require in-person testing, says Casey Marks, chief operating officer at ISC2. The consortium also implemented "the most stringent security protocols available to analyze each result and detect irregularities," including biometric and identity verification.

The testing environment mirrors the most stringent conditions used by licensed professions, such as doctors, to provide the highest security available in the industry, Marks says. Regarding AI use, the fact that ISC2 is exclusively a test-center based for all exams ensures no access to outside resources or technology during exam administration, he adds.

"The candidate, the employer, and every other professional holding that credential depend on the credibility of the process," Marks tells Dark Reading.

Regardless of AI introducing new risks, certifications remain one of the most universal ways for employers to validate a candidate's necessary knowledge and skills when making hiring or promotion decisions, Marks adds.

Carlos agrees but urges programs to have conversations around protecting score validity across the entire process.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

"That includes secure exam design, control during administration, analysis of results, and a clear process for responding to your security concerns," Carlos adds.

A layered approach is crucial because while there are "tools to indicate possible AI use, it's hard to pinpoint exactly." Carlos points to research by Sarah Toton, director of data forensics at Caveon, as an example. Toton conducted an experiment comparing AI and human test taking based on test results and response patterns.

"She has seen some distinct differences in response timing. When someone uses AI, they're often six to 48 times faster compared to an individual test taker," she explains. "That said, AI can get some things wrong sometimes, particularly the questions that involve some realm of human judgment."

In an ironic twist, the same technology people use to cheat on exams is also becoming one of the most in-demand certifications employers rely on to validate real skills.

Many certifications, like ISC2's Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), have and continue to evolve to address how AI is impacting security best practices, Marks says. That's in addition to new AI-specific security certifications that are also entering the market.

For example, the Computing Technology Industry Association launched SecAI+ to help organizations secure, govern, and responsibly integrate AI into their cybersecurity operations.

"As certifications evolve, especially with AI now playing a key role in so many facets of our work, the value of certifications for employers is increasing," Marks adds.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9725. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9724. AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

An organization's ability to quickly recover from a business disruption will be a competitive advantage in an era of AI-driven threats and business enablement.

Commvault SHIFT — Nashville, Tenn. — Enterprise data recovery practices must evolve from a last-resort response to a continuous operational discipline focused on minimizing business disruption and containing the blast radius of cyber incidents as quickly as possible.

That was the central message at Commvault's SHIFT 2026 conference this week, where security executives highlighted the growing importance of making operational resilience a business priority as AI-driven threats and increasingly autonomous business processes complicate the task of maintaining continuity.

"AI is changing the durable advantage you have built for your business, your brand, your supply chain, your data," said Sanjay Mirchandani, president and CEO of Commvault, in a keynote address at the event. "In the AI era, resilience will be your new competitive advantage."

Two developments are driving the trend. On the threat side, AI is giving attackers the ability to automate and accelerate reconnaissance, exploit development, social engineering, and lateral movement. The trend has compressed the time organizations have to detect and contain an intrusion, Mirchandani and other executives at the event noted.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

At the same time, enterprises are increasingly embedding AI into business processes, workflows and decision-making, creating new dependencies on data, applications and autonomous systems.

The result is a more complex operating environment in which a disruption can have wider and faster consequences, making the ability to contain incidents, preserve trusted operations and recover without derailing business activity more important than ever.

Attackers these days are able to move faster with a level of automation not available before, noted Rajeev Kottomtharayil, chief products officer at Commvault. Increasingly, recovery is becoming not just about speed but bringing back clean data. "If everything is under attack, how do we know what to trust? The real goal is to have a clean, safe space to recover even if everything around you has been compromised," Kottomtharayil said.

Business innovation and enablement are also driving the need for greater operational resilience. Resilient operations give organizations the confidence to experiment with AI and put it to work across the business, while ensuring they can recover quickly when something goes wrong, said Pragnesh Dave, head of generative AI and ML sales at AWS. "AI is collapsing the amount of time it takes to move from an idea to an outcome," he said during a keynote session. As a result, the competitive advantage will come not simply from how quickly organizations can turn intelligence into action, but from how quickly they can do so while managing the risks and consequences when those actions sometimes prove wrong.

Related:People Are Getting Weird About AI

Dave pointed to the operations model at Amazon that emphasizes the notion of the "door swinging both ways" when teams try to innovate. It is an approach that has enabled teams at Amazon to code more than four times faster than before, he said.

"The question for everyone is not if something is going to break," he said. Rather, it is about what the blast radius is and the time it takes from when something breaks to recovering to the prior trusted state. "If something goes wrong, you need to be able to recover quickly. You should be able to walk back a decision. Think of your recovery time as your innovation project."

Continuous detection and continuous recovery are going to become a baseline requirement for organizations, argued Peter Diamandis, futurist, entrepreneur, and founder and chairman of the XPRIZE Foundation. Over the next few years, he foresees all organizations harnessing AI to migrate a significant workload to the "digital edge" with humans providing judgement, taste, and oversight. "AI gives us all access to capabilities that were once scarce." The qualities that matter the most will be the speed at which an organization can innovate and that requires standing up capabilities to recover quickly when failures do occur, he said during a keynote address.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

At the same time, recovery is not becoming a substitute for prevention, says Bill O'Connell, chief security officer at Commvault. Both are equally important. But "building the highest walls and the deepest moat" to keep threats out alone is no longer enough. Organizations have to equally focus on building an ability to recover quickly to a trusted state regardless of the reason for a disruption and to thoroughly test that ability before it becomes necessary.

The key to keep in mind is that while AI has dramatically accelerated the pace of change it hasn’t altered the need for traditional, and long-familiar, IT governance and controls around their assets, identities, access, authentication and authentication, O'Connell says. "The IT maintenance and housekeeping elements still matter." When organizations have supercharged tools which they are not entirely sure how to govern, they need to make sure those fundamentals remain in place.

In enabling better resilience, organizations should also evaluate what impact third parties could have on their ability to quickly restore operations, O'Connell says. For years, organizations have used questionnaires and external vendor risk-scoring services to try and assess third-party risk. In the AI era, security teams need to go a step further with their most critical suppliers, he adds. O'Connell suggested organizations have their technical architects work with their counterparts at third-party suppliers to understand how critical services are actually configured and what would happen if a provider experienced a breach or a disruption.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9722. Attackers Say 'Hello' to a Different Scale of Cloud Attack

Researchers dubbed an attack chain "Greeter" after discovering that attackers deliberately covered their trail by leaving "hello" messages in logs.

What began as an exploratory Shodan search for exposed cloud instances has led to the discovery of a broad-ranging AI infrastructure attack campaign that researchers have christened "Greeter." The campaign, which started life as an organized, multistage, systematic attack across cloud providers, reinforces why defenders need to shift their thinking about cloud security to include a layered model built around network access control, data protection, and identity security.

Era Security researchers kicked off the research when the Shodan search engine revealed open Amazon DynamoDB instances where anyone could download data or delete it entirely. They dug a little deeper and found Flowise, a connected open source GenAI development platform, where users can build AI agents powered by large language models (LLMs).

Roughly 90% of the nearly 3,000 scanned Flowise deployments were running unpatched versions vulnerable to a critical code-injection vulnerability, CVE-2024-58351 — and if the researchers could see it, so could attackers. So, Era Security deployed AI-powered honeypots, mostly on Amazon Web Service (AWS), to catch them in action.

Related:LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Honeypot technology is "not like it was before," and attackers don't recognize it's a decoy until they're much further into the environment, according to the Era Security research team. In the past, it took three or fourth months to build a realistic honeypot. Today, it's two hours.

"The most important finding wasn't the exploitation technique itself, but it was what happened after," Naor Talmor, chief technology officer (CTO) at Era Security, tells Dark Reading. What ensued was a repeatable, staged methodology where attackers mapped out privileges and the environment, hunted for credentials, exploited cloud metadata services across multiple providers to escalate access, and then locked in persistence, he explains. Attackers also obfuscated their activity by leaving seemingly benign and fleeting "hello" messages in the logs, making detection much more difficult because it requires team to spend time searching for specific indicators of compromise in the logs. Thus, the researchers gave the campaign the "Greeter" moniker.

The sophisticated techniques and persistence show that Greeter isn't an opportunistic smash-and-grab attack, a script kiddie, or someone who had merely stumbled upon the honeypots, the researchers noted. And, the campaign was deployed across several AWS regions at once, which indicates broader scale and intent.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Era Security warns of the potential scale the campaign could reach, confirming 46 real-world victims so far, based on the number of unauthenticated instances that mirrored the honeypot conditions. The team estimates that at least 50% of those remain connected to the Internet and visible, suggesting at least 20 organizations are currently exposed. The sophistication levels of the the threat actors also speaks to how how valuable the cloud and AI attack surface has become, given the effort required to launch Greeter; this wasn't low-hanging fruit.

The Greeter campaign signals a few shifts across the cloud landscape, including how much easier it's gotten for attackers to go unnoticed in workflows. Much of that is due to AI, which threat actors are using to assist in writing code or orchestrating attack steps, according to the Greeter attack logs.

A decade ago, cloud attacks targeted the Docker API. Threat actors then began exploiting workloads, escaping containers to reach the cloud's metadata server underneath, and exploiting service accounts from there, the researchers explain. While attackers are following a similar pattern, they are now using AI infrastructure as the new way to establish persistence.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Researchers agree that the end goal on each instance was to grab cloud credentials and perform lateral movement within a targeted organization.

Meanwhile, attribution remains quite challenging. When the researchers drilled down to the code and techniques, they started to see Chinese characters, though that could be a false flag. Still, a nation-state culprit would make since, because the notion of seeing an "entire orchestration, not even a big cybercrime group could execute that," according to Era Security.

The current velocity of vulnerability exploitation is nothing like the researchers have seen in the past, which puts immense pressure on organizations' traditional patching cycles. This played out just over the past few weeks alone, as security teams raced to fix PHP2Shell and OpenSSH, searching workloads one by one for flaws. However, the Greeter campaign shows a defense challenge for cloud security that's bigger than fixing any specific vulnerability.

Everyone needs to assume a breach now, warns Talmor, adding how if it's not a vulnerability, it may be leaked credentials or an exposed API. Organizations need to design security programs around the cloud to be ready for all of the above, he advises, adopting defense-in-depth.

"A lot of companies adopt that, but they don't really practice it," he notes.

The researchers say organizations can detect this kind of attack much faster if teams monitor for enumeration activity to close gaps before attackers find them. When applications or chat tools are installed, logging can be activated and streamed to a separate location so that even if attackers do delete a device's local history, the logs remain stored in the cloud.

Researchers also noted that this should be monitored closely in critical environments, especially where crown jewels or critical applications are involved, adding that organizations can have dozens or hundreds of accounts depending on the size.

"To be clear, we aren't saying, 'Stop caring about misconfigurations or stop caring about vulnerabilities," Talmor says, warning that patch management is a game "we are losing" that requires organizations to secure their environment layer by layer.

#9721. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9720. AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

この対策パッケージには、官民合同のサイバー対応チーム、経済省が主導するAI専門チーム、および政府の新たな能動的サイバー防衛権限の行使に関する裁量の拡大が含まれている。

Translation provided by Dark Reading's internal AI translation tool.

日本においてサイバー攻撃や情報漏洩が急増していることを受け、日本政府は、攻撃に迅速に対応し、インフラのセキュリティを強化するための産官の専門家チームを設立することを目的とした、100億円（6,300万ドル）規模の緊急サイバーセキュリティ対策パッケージを可決した。

この戦略の4つの柱には、サイバー防衛へのAI導入を含む基礎的なサイバーセキュリティ対策の全国的な徹底、国内のサイバー捜査能力の強化、サイバー攻撃の被害者への支援拡充、そして民間企業と連携してサイバー攻撃に共同で対応することが含まれている。

高市早苗首相は、国のサイバーレジリエンス（回復力）を高めるため、これらのサイバーセキュリティ対策を「迅速かつ効果的に」実施するよう求めた。

「今この瞬間も、不正アクセスや情報漏洩の事案が後を絶たず、人々の日常生活や企業活動に多大な影響を及ぼしている」と、高市早苗首相は11月6日に緊急対策パッケージを発表した際の声明で述べた。「政府のあらゆる資源を動員し、サイバー攻撃への対応能力を全面的に強化していこう。」

サイバー攻撃の急増は、日本企業や政府機関に甚大な被害をもたらしている。サイバーセキュリティ企業（旧トレンドマイクロ）であるTrendAIのデータによると、2026年の最初の9か月間で600件以上のサイバーセキュリティインシデントが公表され、2025年通年の594件を上回った。公表されている報告数は控えめな推計に過ぎない。日本の個人情報保護監督機関は、4月から10月中旬にかけて2,094件の情報漏洩事案を記録しており（原文は日本語）、これも2025年度通年の総件数を上回っている。

他の地域ではAIが攻撃者を支援しているものの、サイバーセキュリティ企業TrendAIの脅威調査共同責任者であるライアン・フローレス氏は、脅威に関する声明の中で、インシデントの増加と攻撃者によるAIの利用との間に明確な関連性は確認されていないと述べた。

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

「サイバー攻撃は世界的に増加しており、その結果として侵害やデータ漏洩も増加しています」と同氏は述べた。「AIが直接関与しているわけではないかもしれませんが、攻撃者が標的を見つけたり、操作を自動化したりするのを支援するAIの能力により、サイバー攻撃は大規模化しています。組織は、被害に遭う確率を下げるために、サイバーリスクを低減し、脆弱性を解消する必要があります。」

最近の侵害事例には、冷凍食品大手のニチレイやビール・食品大手のアサヒに対するランサムウェア攻撃、およびGMOインターネットグループを標的としたデータ侵害などが含まれる。これらの攻撃の多くは犯罪的な性質を持つが、盗まれた情報が他の犯罪グループや国家主体のアクターによって、日本の国民に対して悪用される可能性があることが懸念されていると、日本の通信大手NTTのチーフ・サイバーセキュリティ・ストラテジスト、松原美穂子氏は指摘する。

「攻撃者が十分な個人情報を収集・集約できれば、個人の嗜好から経済活動に至るまで、日本国民の詳細なプロファイルを構築できる」と同氏は述べる。「そのデータは、世論を操作したり、日本の機関に対する信頼を損なわせたりするための標的型偽情報キャンペーンなど、日本に対する影響工作に利用される可能性がある」

日本政府は、緊急資金を活用して、サイバーセキュリティ体制全体を強化するための4つの広範な取り組みを推進する意向だ。閣僚会議の公表された議事録によると、政府は、最近の多くの情報漏洩は適切なセキュリティ対策によって防ぐことができたはずだと指摘し、最初の取り組みとして、各組織が基本的なサイバーセキュリティ対策を確実に実施するよう促すとしている。

2つ目の主要な取り組みは、調査および情報収集能力を向上させ、より精度の高い分析を可能にし、その結果を国民に提供することで、攻撃への備えを強化することである。第三に、政府はサイバー攻撃への対応を強化し、国際的なパートナーシップを構築するとともに、積極的なサイバー防衛措置を実施する。最後に、政府は被害者を支援する能力とインフラを整備し、市民が損害を回復し、企業が事業を継続できるようにする計画だ。

「被害を受けた組織や個人が迷うことなく支援を受けられるよう、利用しやすい相談窓口や専門家による直接的な支援を拡充し、二次被害を防ぐための情報共有を強化する」と、日本の議事録には記されている。「また、官民の専門家を柔軟に派遣するための全国的な仕組みの構築にも着手する」

10月1日、日本の「積極的サイバー防衛法」が施行され、警察や自衛隊（SDF）に対し、日本の国家安全保障にリスクをもたらすあらゆるサイバー攻撃に対して強力な措置を講じる権限が与えられた。

「多くの国が、日本がいかなる種類のサイバー攻撃に対して、どれほどの速さで、どの程度の強度で対応できるのかを知りたがっているだろう」とNTTの松原氏は述べ、次のように付け加えた。「この緊急対策パッケージは……法律の枠組みを経済全体にわたる実用的な能力へと転換し、攻撃の可能性が高まる中、あらゆる規模の組織が攻撃を予防、検知、対応できるよう準備するために必要である。」

しかし、この資金はあくまで第一歩に過ぎず、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの投資を継続するには、さらなる資金が必要になると同氏は指摘する。

「この対策パッケージの重要な点は、サイバーセキュリティを個々の組織に完全に任せておくことはできないという認識が示されていることだ」と松原氏は述べる。「セキュリティ評価やインシデント対応、復旧支援といった形の政府による支援が、大きな違いを生むことができる。」

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9719. My Local AI Agent Needed a Bigger Brain, So I Gave It a Decentralized GPU

AI Engineer. I ship LLM systems, autonomous agents, and inference pipelines — then write about what I learned

Nosana is an open-source GPU cloud for AI and high-performance workloads, offering lower-cost instant compute.

AI Engineer. I ship LLM systems, autonomous agents, and inference pipelines — then write about what I learned

Nosana is an open-source GPU cloud for AI and high-performance workloads, offering lower-cost instant compute.

this is my second progress update for the Decentralize AI Hackathon by HackerNoon and Nosana.

In my first article, I Built a Local AI Linux Assistant That Doesn't Rely on the Cloud, I introduced zkzkAgent: an AI agent that manages a Linux machine through plain language and runs entirely on my own hardware with Ollama.

That is still how it works by default. But running everything locally has a ceiling, and I kept hitting it.

To test the integration in real work, I switched to the 27B model on Nosana and gave zkzkAgent a task: create a new project called zkzk_ai, a calculator web app with a FastAPI backend and an HTML, CSS, and JavaScript frontend, and open it in VS Code.

The classifier sent the request to the planner (`NEEDS_PLANNING`). The planner wrote a 9-step plan, including the full content of every file, and then stopped and waited for me:

Once I approved the plan, the executor got to work. It made 10 tool calls, one at a time, across 10 graph iterations (with a maximum of 15).

Wrote static/index.html (2,396 characters)

Wrote static/style.css (1,563 characters)

Wrote static/script.js (2,655 characters)

Nothing complicated happens behind the scenes. The model running on Nosana picks a tool; that tool executes on my machine, and the result is sent back to the model.

To make this clearer, here's an actual example from the execution log (trimmed for readability):Each call follows the same loop. The model on Nosana picks the next tool, the tool runs on my machine, and the result goes back into the conversation. In the log, one turn of that loop looks like this (trimmed):

Next, I asked: "Can you change the zkzk_ai Calculator to be zkzk?" The classifier sent this to the planner as well, which wrote a 7-step plan. After I approved it, the agent read static/index.html and then changed the name in three places: the page title and heading, the FastAPI app title, and the README. It did not touch the calculator logic.

I started the app with `uvicorn app:app`. The page loaded, and the calculator API answered:

Across both requests, every model call in the saved log, 18 in total, went to `inference.nosana.com` and returned `200 OK`. Every file write, command, and app launch happened locally.

I reviewed the code the agent wrote, and tested the backend directly:

- No eval. Expressions are parsed with Python's ast module, and only numbers, parentheses, and `+ - * / // % **` are allowed. When I sent __import__("os"), it was rejected with "Unsupported expression element: Call".

- Clear errors. Division by zero and complex results (such as (-1)**0.5) return a readable message instead of crashing.

- Input limits. Expressions are capped at 500 characters in both the browser and the API.

- Keyboard support. Enter evaluates, Backspace deletes, Esc clears and `^` types a power.

The code is on GitHub at [zkzkGamal/calculator], and the full run log is in the [zkzkAgent repo]

My first article was about an agent that doesn't rely on the cloud. This update doesn't change that. It adds a choice. Private or sensitive work stays on local Ollama, where nothing leaves the machine. Heavy planning can use a much larger model on Nosana's network instead of a centralized provider. In both modes, the tools, the files, and the final yes stay with me.

1. A real benchmark. Run the same five tasks on the local 2B model and on the 27B model on Nosana, and measure success rate, tool calls, time, tokens, and cost. Numbers instead of impressions.

2. Hybrid routing. Because the graph has separate nodes, each node can use its own model. The classifier and chat replies are short and could stay on a small local model, while the planner and executor use Nosana. Plain conversations would then never leave the machine.

3. Automatic fallback. If Nosana can't be reached, switch to local Ollama automatically, the same way the agent already turns Wi-Fi back on by itself.

4. Close the safety gaps. Enforce plan-level confirmations. Also put `run_command` behind a confirmation or an allow-list: today it can run any shell command, and with a remote model choosing the arguments, that matters more than before.

5. Fix the calculator bug with the agent doing the fix.

zkzkAgent: https://github.com/zkzkGamal/zkzkAgent The calculator it built: https://github.com/zkzkGamal/calculator

Full Nosana run log: https://github.com/zkzkGamal/zkzkAgent/blob/main/docs/nosana-run-2026-10-25.log

#9718. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9717. Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The package adds public-private cyber responders, an AI-focused team run by the economic ministry, and more leeway to use the government's new active cyber-defense powers.

To read this story in Japanese, please click here (translation by our internal AI tool).

With Japan facing a surge in cyberattacks and breaches, the Japanese government has passed a ¥10 billion ($63 million) emergency cybersecurity package aimed at establishing teams of industry and government experts to quickly respond to attacks and better secure its infrastructure.

The four pillars of the strategy include thoroughly implementing basic cybersecurity measures country-wide, including adopting AI for cyber-defense, strengthening the nation's cyber-investigations capabilities, better supporting the victims of cyberattacks, and partnering with private industry to jointly respond to cyberattacks.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called for the cybersecurity measures to be implemented "promptly and effectively" to enhance the nation's cyber resilience.

"Even at this very moment, incidents of unauthorized access and information leaks continue to occur, significantly affecting people's daily lives and business activities," Takaichi said in a published statement announcing the emergency package on November 6. "Let us mobilize the full resources of the Government to strengthen Japan's overall capabilities to respond to cyberattacks."

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

While AI has aided attackers elsewhere, TrendAI has not established a firm link between the increases and the use of AI by attackers, Ryan Flores, co-lead for threat research at TrendAI, a cybersecurity firm, said in a statement on the threats.

"Cyberattacks are increasing globally, and so are the breaches and data leaks as a result," he said. "While AI might not be directly involved, its ability to help the attackers find targets and automate their operations makes cyberattacks scalable. Organizations need to shrink their cyber exposure and close the vulnerabilities in order to lower the odds of being victimized."

Recent compromises include ransomware attacks on business, such as frozen food giant Nichirei and brewery and food giant Asahi, and data breaches targeting GMO Internet Group. While many of the attacks are criminal in nature, the worry is that the stolen information could be used by other criminal groups and nation-state actors against the Japanese public, says Mihoko Matsubara, chief cybersecurity strategist for Japanese telecom giant NTT.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

"If attackers can collect and aggregate enough personal information, they can build detailed profiles of Japanese citizens, from personal preferences to economic activities," she says. "That data could potentially be used for influence operations against Japan, such as targeted disinformation campaigns to manipulate public opinion or undermine trust in Japanese institutions."

The Japanese government intends to use the emergency funding to pursue four broad initiatives to improve its overall cybersecurity posture. Pointing out that many recent breaches could have been prevented by good hygiene, the government's first initiative is to ensure organizations are implementing basic cybersecurity measures, according to the published Japanese notes of the ministerial meeting.

The second major initiative is to improve investigation and information collection capabilities, allowing better analysis that can then be delivered to the public to better prepare them for attacks. Third, the government will strengthen its response to cyberattacks, establishing international partnerships and implementing active cyber-defense measures. Finally, the government plans to create the capability and infrastructure to support victims so that citizens can recover damages and businesses can remain operational.

Related:UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

"Accessible consultation points and direct expert support will be expanded so that affected organizations and individuals can connect to support without confusion, and communication to prevent secondary harm will be strengthened," the Japanese notes stated. "Work will also begin on building a nationwide mechanism for flexibly dispatching public- and private-sector specialists."

On October 1, Japan's Active Cyber Defense legislation came into effect, authorizing the police and the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) to take strong measures against any cyberattacks that pose a risk to Japan’s national security.

"Many countries would be keen to learn how quickly Japan could respond to which kind of cyberattacks, and with what level of intensity," says NTT's Matsubara, adding: "This emergency package is ... necessary to translate the law’s framework into practical capabilities across the broader economy, preparing organizations of all sizes to prevent, detect and respond to attacks as they become increasingly likely."

However, the funds are only enough to get started, and more will be necessary to continue Japan's investment in cybersecurity, she says.

"The important aspect about this package is that it recognizes that cybersecurity cannot be left entirely to individual organizations," Matsubara says. "Government assistance, in the form of security assessments and incident response or recovery support, can make a difference."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).
